### 2026-11-18 — Grammar production construction and its tests move to Tower

Scope agreed with the user: this task owns grammar construction; independent
tasks own formatting and interpretation. Those implementations were not edited.
The user also made measured performance an acceptance criterion and asked that
new tests be written in Tower rather than adding more C++ to translate. This
supersedes the first draft's native test fixture: that uncommitted C++ test file
was removed, and the fixtures/checks now live in `scaffolding/tests/syntax-emission.tower`.

Implemented `compiler/syntax-emission.tower` and switched production `syntax.cpp`
to it for both ordinary revisions and replacement-template parser construction.
Tower now assigns literal IDs, avoids generated-name collisions (including names
of pending definitions), emits ordinary/repeated/captured productions and token
exclusions, builds template token wrappers, and computes declaration reachability
and leading token/literal sets. Production order, generated flags, capture roles,
and user-alternative/provenance mappings preserve the previous implementation.
Template hole insertion, template checking/expansion and session/environment
ownership remain native; this port does not claim those stages are complete.

Construction directly creates the existing shared Rule/Reference/String/Range
entities, using Tower's entity/component APIs and existing payload definitions.
There is no second AST, serialized instruction stream or authoritative grammar
model. Hash tables, FIRST sets, provenance/name views and queues are disposable
revision indexes. A small `entity_create_related` primitive allocates in the
existing entity's store. Parser component types now register their existing Tower
payload size/finalizer when first requested; the native creation adapter uses
that same finalizer, so Tower can create the components directly without hidden
native grammar-building algorithms. The `SyntaxEmissionInput` ABI borrows shared
source entities; source declarations are not modified. A failed emission frees
its indexes, leaves partial output children owned by its output root, and the
caller discards that root. Existing revisions remain usable.

Performance-related choices: intern names in a hash index, use one monotonically
increasing helper ordinal with exact collision checks, and mark token exclusions
through that index instead of comparing every literal with every exclusion.
The exclusion mark identifies the immutable source term, so repeated emission
of the same term needs neither a global clear nor an overflowing generation
counter. Removed duplicate native reservations of every rule/token name; Tower
already reserves them and supplies the complete used-name index back to the
temporary native revision adapter. This is construction-time work only; source
recognition retains the existing LR/DFA control and does not gain a search or
backtracking path. Rebuilding tables after successive grammar edits is still a
separate optimization opportunity.

Bootstrap accounting: `bootstrap/syntax-emission-seed.cpp` retains the prior C++
algorithm as the seed/stage1 and separately renamed differential reference.
It is not an additional production implementation or a third-party exemption.
Its native ABI adaptation, the production borrowed-view adapter, native test
runner and component registration remain migration debt. New functional test
logic is Tower: the existing native runner merely supplies component type IDs,
invokes the Tower test entry and reports its failure index. Test-only Tower code
is appended only for `TOWER_PARSER_ONLY`, not shipped in browser/compiler builds.
An eventual validated portable Tower compiler distribution must replace the
owned bootstrap sources; that endpoint has not been reached by this port.

Validation and trials (Windows/PowerShell, WSL Orchestral-Revng, LLVM 19,
WASI SDK 34, Node 21.7.3):

- Tower fixtures compare exact shared parser component trees, token IDs,
  generated flags, captures, production indexes, helper origins, literal/name
  metadata, declaration starts and template wrapper names against the retained
  native algorithm. Cases include Bedrock, absent Statement, empty alternatives,
  collisions with generated spellings, skipped/contextual tokens, cyclic and
  nullable references, all repetition kinds, captures and large exclusions.
- 400 deterministic generated graphs are checked in ordinary and template modes.
  The Tower test generator uses an explicit u32 LCG (seed 1162692948), replacing
  the draft's native mt19937 fixture. The 512-literal exclusion fixture exercises
  multiple repeated sets. Failure injection sweeps every allocation until
  success on representative ordinary/template inputs and checks live allocation
  counts after disposing partial roots. The earlier native fixture also passed
  before being removed, but it is not the maintained test implementation.
- Linux CTest with ASan/UBSan passed 4/4; optimized Windows parser/compiler checks
  passed. The sanitizers instrument the native harness/adapters, not every
  instruction in generated Tower objects. The failure/parity suites execute the
  production Tower implementation on both targets.
- Native compiler, Wasm frontend and Wasm LLVM/cross reactors built successfully.
  The canonical formatter check covers 46 Tower files, including this new
  implementation and the new Tower tests.
- Early compilation failures identified reserved names (`token`, `skip`,
  `expected`) used as internal identifiers, unsupported member access directly
  on a returned call, and bool bitwise expressions in test scaffolding. These
  were rewritten using ordinary Foundation declarations/operands; no special
  grammar or semantic features were added for the port.
- Narrowing computed terminal ordinals generated an unwanted `tower_trap`
  dependency. Explicit width masks preserve the previous uint32 truncation
  semantics and allow the backend to prove the conversions safe. Test-generated
  ASCII ordinals use explicit masks as well. No trap import was added.
- One early four-target bootstrap comparison saw different source revisions
  because the exclusion-index edit rebuilt the composed module during the run
  (72-byte versus 80-byte name entries in the IR). This was an invalid trial,
  not evidence of host nondeterminism. Final comparisons must run with inputs
  frozen for the entire seed/Tower pair.

## 2026-11-18 — Port interpreter execution into Tower (isolated worktree)

Started from `f034216` on `port/interpreter-tower` in
`C:/Sandbox/tower-interpreter`. The original checkout and `todo.txt` were not
modified. Build products are under that worktree's `build/` and the separate
WSL cache `/home/trevo/.cache/tower-interpreter/{native,tests,asan,wasm-tests}`.
No merge, push, publication, UI/worker, grammar construction, formatting engine,
type-checker, shared foundation component-layout, or LLVM-lowering change is
part of this port.

Implemented execution in `scaffolding/compiler/interpreter.tower`: target-byte
memory access; aligned first-fit allocation, splitting, coalescing, reallocation
and free; scalar arithmetic/conversion; raw target-address calculation; literal
storage; function frames and foreign calls; resumable expression tasks; loops,
break/continue/returns; output formatting and truncation. The implementation reads
the original FoundationNode components. It introduces no instruction stream,
public bytecode, replacement program graph, checked pointer handle, or executable
memory requirement. Pointer widths still come from the guest's explicit target;
the interpreter's own host ABI is a distinct layout, verified in the tests.

The C++ CoreMachine source is now an adapter for public methods, host containers,
existing shared type/component queries, diagnostic-string storage, and callback
marshalling. Container bridges do not choose operations, schedule evaluation,
calculate addresses, merge allocations, or format guest output. Ordered neighbor
queries return ordinary container observations; coalescing remains Tower code.
Public source-level CoreMachine members/methods remain available. Its scalar
state is a shared ABI base; derived frame/task counts and error/cache flags remove
repeated host calls. Counts/error state refresh on public step entry and foreign
callback return. All native callers must rebuild against the updated header.

The composed interpreter input reuses FoundationType/FoundationNode declarations
from `foundation-nodes.tower`, and generates kind/operator/scalar tag spellings
from the existing C++ enums. It does not duplicate those schemas or introduce
new semantic operation definitions. This is temporary source composition until
imports exist; the declaration boundary is checked. Task-phase and bootstrap
limits have static assertions; state size and every field offset are compared
against the actual Tower-compiled layout for native and Wasm targets.

Production `towerc`, parser/core tests, and the browser reactor link the Tower
interpreter object. `towerc-seed` and `towerc-stage1` deliberately retain the
original execution algorithms in `bootstrap/interpreter-seed.cpp` to avoid a
bootstrap dependency cycle. That same frozen implementation is independently
renamed for differential testing. It is retained migration debt, not a completed
pure-Tower bootstrap. Native std::vector/std::map/string/function storage, the
host allocation primitives, shared native type queries/component accessors, and
the fatal internal `tower_trap` adapter also remain migration debt. Guest errors
are checked/diagnosed by Tower; that fatal adapter is for compiler-owned runtime
invariant failures. Integration with other ports must provide only one definition
of the compiler-owned `tower_trap` symbol.

Experiments and corrections:

- A direct translation initially failed because `skip` is reserved, boolean
  bitwise operations are disallowed, and `bits` cannot change integer widths.
  Used an ordinary local name, Tower boolean helpers, and explicit masking before
  narrowing conversion. No grammar/type-checker exception was added.
- Linking the first Tower object exposed its `tower_trap` dependency; supplied
  the small fatal adapter rather than weakening checked operation semantics.
- Differential fixture corrections respected Foundation's existing syntax:
  binary return/argument expressions require locals; pointer reinterpretation
  requires target-width integers; a negative index uses an explicitly typed
  signed variable (a bare index literal receives usize context).
- WASI reference linking initially needed `-fno-exceptions` on the reference
  library as well as the test executable. Corrected only test registration.
- The first native loop sample regressed: Tower 73.39 ms versus C++ 53.43 ms.
  Direct scalar-state access reduced the Tower sample to 64.65 ms; reusing already
  fetched shared components reduced it to 55.10 ms. Subsequent changes bypass
  provably empty statement caches, avoid redundant FinishValue probes, defer
  component lookup until after a cache hit check, specialize container bridges,
  and combine ordered-neighbor observations. They preserve step counts, caches,
  task order, output, errors and memory at suspension boundaries. These are
  execution/index optimizations, not new program semantics. Performance remains
  workload/target dependent; in particular Wasm allocation is not a demonstrated
  speedup over the native reference.
- Exhaustive full-memory comparisons during thousands of identical infinite-loop
  suspensions made the first WASI harness unnecessarily slow; those trials were
  stopped. The final suite compares the first 128 budgeted steps of those loops,
  then separately crosses the output limit with a larger slice. Finite programs
  still compare at every suspension and must terminate (including error exits).
- Windows Node 22.23.4's native `node:wasi` binding reproducibly terminated with
  process code -1073741819 (access violation), sometimes during literal-output
  tests, without a Wasm exception. Disabling Wasm tier-up did not resolve it.
  Wrapping/logging the WASI imports allowed the complete suite to pass. The exact
  native-host cause is NOT established. The checked-in runner instead uses the
  project's existing portable TowerWASI host, which passes the suite and matches
  the playground's host path; no host implementation or worker was changed.
- An initial broader Node test command included raw-memory/inference/templates
  suites that require a separate LLVM reactor and failed at missing-artifact
  imports. No result is claimed for those suites. The focused reactor tests and
  freshly built native LLVM comparisons below cover the executed paths.

Reproduction (WSL Ubuntu, clang++ 21.1.8, installed LLVM 19; WASI SDK 34.0 with
clang 23.1.0; Windows Node 22.23.4). From `/mnt/c/Sandbox/tower-interpreter`:

cmake -S . -B "$cache/native" -G Ninja -DTOWER_NATIVE=ON \

The differential suite runs 26 source fixtures with budgets 1/7/1000 and guest
pointer widths 4/8 (156 runs), plus direct allocation-fragmentation trials.
It compares full target memory, allocations/free blocks, output and truncation,
errors/offsets, steps, frame/task stacks, and per-statement value/address caches.
Coverage includes recursion/stack exhaustion, nested calls/effects and captured
assignment destinations, loops/break/continue, literals, negative indexing,
overlapping copy, reallocation success/failure/zero, raw addresses, foreign
callbacks that mutate/relocate memory or fail, arithmetic wrap/division overflow,
conversion errors, zero budgets and infinite-loop suspension. Layout offsets
are checked under both actual compiler hosts. ASan/UBSan instrument the native
adapter/reference/compiler, not the precompiled Tower LLVM object; their passing
results must not be described as full instrumentation of Tower code.

Next migration work: replace native storage/ABI helpers with Tower-owned runtime
containers and callbacks while preserving the source-level interface, retire the
seed after a validated Tower-built portable bootstrap exists, and improve the
allocation-heavy Wasm path without changing step/effect contracts. The shared
schema composition and runtime trap symbol are explicit integration points for
parallel grammar/formatting ports. No MSVC/macOS validation or end-to-end browser
UI timing is claimed here.

Final review correction: empty literal components can have a null name buffer
(the native CoreName::c_str supplies an empty string in that case). Copy only the
nonempty payload and explicitly write the target NUL terminator in Tower; the
literal fixture now includes empty strings. This was an implementation defect
found during review and fixed before committing, not a change to raw-pointer
semantics. The final differential suite covers this path on native and Wasm.

## 2026-11-18 — Canonical formatter moved to Tower (base f034216)

Implemented in isolated branch port/canonical-formatter-tower and worktree
C:\Sandbox\tower-formatter. The original workspace and todo.txt are untouched.
A second, unmodified detached worktree at C:\Sandbox\tower-formatter-reference
pins f034216 for the controlled performance comparison. All generated objects,
downloaded tools, npm cache, logs and reactors are under the formatter worktree's
build directory. No merge, push or publication was performed.

The production tower_format and tower_format_source entry points now invoke
compiler/format.tower, format-foundation.tower, format-grammar.tower and
format-source.tower. These modules read the existing FoundationNode, SyntaxNode
and ParserMatchData components directly through entity_component_get/data.
There is no additional authoritative AST, operation model or program format.
Temporary source-token positions and spacing flags are derived layout data, as
in the preceding implementation. Foundation and source output share the same
byte writer, escaping, identifiers, indentation, newlines and span machinery.
Grammar declarations dispatch through that same engine and preserve declaration
order, = versus |=, captures/repetition, terminal sets, contextual tokens,
replacement body bytes, comments and optional provenance. Source formatting
continues to consume lexer-provided comments and original parser matches.
The existing parse/format equivalence guard in syntax.cpp was not changed.

Moved decimal conversion, quoting, identifier escaping, canonical reserved-name
selection, grammar wrapping, type/expression/statement traversal, affix and call
spacing, blank lines and ordered output-span creation to Tower. Reused existing
type/operation definitions through small C bridges for CoreKind predicates,
builtin/operator spellings and scalar type properties/names. Type layout and
all shared component layouts remain unchanged. The native wrapper only supplies
component kinds, adapts ownership/results and queries those shared definitions.
Identifier decoding already lived in Tower's syntax reader and still uses it.

The old formatter is retained in scaffolding/bootstrap/format-seed.cpp, with
only include-path adjustments. It builds the seed and stage1 compilers and
serves as the independently named differential reference. It is explicitly
migration debt, not a second production formatter. Normal towerc and browser
reactors link the Tower implementation; parser tests always compare it with the
reference. TOWER_FORMAT_DIFFERENTIAL=ON also enables reference checks in the
browser reactor. Checks compare exact bytes and every ordered (begin,end,source)
triple, including nested spans. Production builds leave that option OFF and
contain no reference formatter. Build/test registration is kept in a separate
commit from formatter implementation and tests.

Debugging/failed trials:
- Initial authoring used unquoted token/skip local names and bitwise operations
  on bool. Foundation correctly rejected both. Renamed the locals and used
  ordinary Tower boolean helper functions; did not extend the foundation.
- The first native suite found an entity-allocation-count change while formatting
  Bedrock. Eagerly obtaining core_component_type registered a permanent foundation
  component even on grammar-only calls. Made its registration lazy, matching the
  preceding formatter's behavior. Native ownership checks subsequently pass.
- A contextual-token fixture initially kept an Identifier-led Statement
  alternative active and was tokenized as an assignment. Restricted that fixture's
  active Statement to the contextual token; no parser changes were made.
- The first broad Node run lacked build/linking/wasm-fixture.a. Built the existing
  foreign-fixture.c with the SDK and llvm-ar, then reran successfully.
- The initial large benchmark hit runToEnd's UI-only 1,024-construct budget.
  The dedicated benchmark now uses a bounded direct step loop without changing
  the playground. Also rejected its initial 5,000-root foundation timing:
  compilation exceeds the foundation module limit and returns empty formatting.
  That fixture now measures only source formatting; all measured outputs must
  be nonempty and agree in text and spans before timing.

After the user's explicit request to make Tower faster where possible, added
measured optimizations with stated eligibility:
- Check comment ordering once. Ordered lexer trivia uses binary lower bounds
  rather than rescanning every comment for every root/statement. Unsorted
  caller-supplied comments retain the preceding full-scan behavior and order;
  a reversed-comment differential test covers this fallback.
- Skip sorting already ordered source-token positions. Retain O(n log n)
  heapsort for interleaved comments or otherwise unordered input.
- Batch repeated bytes and decimal digits, and append runs of unescaped string
  bytes rather than appending each byte individually.
- Group canonical reserved names by length and stop after a match.
No optimization changes evaluation, entity identity, trivia or source spans.
These are workload-specific performance improvements, not a universal speed
guarantee or an excuse to introduce new semantic representations.

Performance: rebuilt f034216 in the detached reference worktree using exactly

build/formatter-reference directory. Ran
node scaffolding/tests/format-benchmark.mjs build/formatter-reference/tower.wasm

the existing reparsing/equivalence guard; foundation timing includes host JSON
output. This is Node-hosted Wasm, not browser typing latency or native timings.

Controlled-run medians, original C++ -> Tower (milliseconds):
- 10 declarations: source 0.2568 -> 0.2525; foundation 0.0111 -> 0.0107.
- 1,000 declarations: source 18.9964 -> 19.3102; foundation 0.5689 -> 0.5402.
- 5,000 declarations with comments: source 143.7436 -> 116.2151 (~19% faster).
- 200 long strings: source 17.1277 -> 17.6152; foundation 3.0697 -> 1.5050
  (~51% faster).
The repeat retained ~19% improvement for comment-heavy source and ~50% for
long-string foundation output. Small/common source cases varied around parity;
one source-string run improved ~16% while the other regressed ~3%, so no stable
claim is made for it. The consistent large-case wins justify the changes;
near-noise differences do not establish that all Tower formatting is faster.

bootstrap removal has an integration dependency and cannot honestly be called
independent of the completed compiler):

1. Frontend — this machine. Port replacement template checking/expansion first,

   stream orchestration, parser diagnostics/recovery, highlighting and Bedrock
   seed construction. Own syntax.cpp/.hpp, parser.cpp/.hpp, bedrock.cpp,

   provenance and grammar-update contracts. LR/DFA/regex algorithms already run
   in Tower; do not recreate them. No semantic compiler, backend, host-driver or
   interpreter/formatter implementation changes in this task.

2. Semantic compiler/type system — external task. Own core.cpp, core-nodes.cpp,
   the semantic declarations in core.hpp/foundation-values.hpp and corresponding
   Foundation components and new semantic Tower modules/tests. Port module/local
   binding, type/layout resolution, operands/operations/calls/control-flow checks,
   template/type-constructor integration and diagnostics. Keep current shared
   node layouts/operation IDs and query contracts stable while other owners use
   them; coordinate a necessary ABI change explicitly instead of silently changing
   it. Do not redesign the language or take the formatter/interpreter algorithm,
   frontend, backend or driver work. Use compiler-owned entities directly, not
   another semantic IR. CoreMachine declarations belong to task 4.

3. LLVM/backend integration — external task. Own llvm-engine.cpp/.hpp,
   llvm-backend.cpp, llvm-wasi.cpp and corresponding Tower backend modules/tests.

   emission, disassembly and browser-native linker orchestration. Preserve
   existing target/ABI/semantic contracts and share the same Foundation entities.
   LLVM/lld implementations remain third-party; owned glue is still migration

   entry points rather than a permanent custom native shim. Task 4 owns driver,

4. Host/runtime/bootstrap integration — external task. Own driver.cpp,

   residual registration/storage/callback bridges (including core-machine.cpp,

### 2026-11-19 — Host/runtime ownership: Tower CLI and compiler allocation policy

The requested host/runtime/bootstrap workstream starts from integrated master
586078b, pulled with `git pull --rebase` before any work. Created
`port/host-runtime-tower`. No task 1–3 algorithms were rewritten and todo.txt
was not modified. The user's follow-up explicitly asks to avoid new C++: new
behavior and functional host tests are Tower; native changes are interface views,
forwarding into Tower, isolation of already-existing bootstrap behavior, and one
reference-test portability correction. This is an incremental host port, NOT
completion of the requested self-hosting compiler/distribution.

Implemented:

- `scaffolding/host/driver-options.tower` owns CLI parsing, defaults, option
  ordering, early help, borrowed argv text, repeated link inputs, diagnostics
  classification and cleanup. Help text also lives in Tower. Stage1 and production
  drivers call this implementation. The original CLI loop remains guarded by
  TOWER_BOOTSTRAP_HOST only in towerc-seed; source loading, diagnostic output,
  timing, filesystem/process calls and linker orchestration still live in the
  native driver. No new C++ parser was written as an intermediate implementation.
- `scaffolding/host/memory.tower` owns allocation-size overflow, zero-size release,
  live-buffer/call accounting and one-shot/delayed allocation-failure injection.
  Overflow does not consume an injection; injected failure precedes even zero-size
  release, matching the previous host. Failure preserves the caller's allocation.
  Null instrumentation state selects production behavior. Compiler allocator
  forwarding and the host libc calls remain in compiler-memory.cpp. This does not
  change guest raw-pointer semantics or claim new guest memory-safety guarantees.
- The original allocator is preserved, with provenance, as
  bootstrap/compiler-memory-seed.cpp and linked ONLY into towerc-seed. The seed
  builds the Tower host object, so stage1 and later consumers can use it without
  a cyclic build dependency. TowerHost.cmake/ComposeHost.cmake compose the sources;
  browser builds omit the unused CLI implementation. The bootstrap comparison
  script now covers the host object on four target triples.
- `tests/host-runtime.tower` exercises defaults, all value options, missing values,
  repeated options/link order, help ordering, option-looking values, failure and
  double-disposal cleanup, count*size overflow, zero-size free, preserved bytes
  after realloc/failure, failure reset/countdown, and production allocation.
  The existing parser command merely calls the Tower test entry point. Functional
  test logic was not added in C++.

Boundary findings and integration fixes:

1. llvm-engine.cpp currently rejects all library top-level statements, including
   module variables, and reserves tower_allocate/reallocate/deallocate/print/trap
   against source definitions. These are concrete blockers to directly replacing
   the remaining entry-symbol/state adapters with Tower definitions under today's
   backend contract. This work uses explicit state and a temporary C ABI instead
   of changing task 3's backend or inventing a second runtime ABI. The libc symbol
   names also overlap built-in alloc/free/realloc spellings; foreign binding and
   runtime-definition contracts need coordination before removing those bridges.
2. The first CLI compile failed at boolean bitwise OR: Tower requires integer
   operands there. Replaced the two boolean combinations with ordinary Tower
   conditionals; no language/semantic/compiler change was needed.
3. A complete WASI parser test build exposed a pre-existing C++ reference lambda
   returning SIZE_MAX (unsigned int) on one path and size_t (unsigned long) on
   another, despite equal widths on wasm32. Added an explicit size_t return type
   to that lambda in bootstrap/lr-analysis-seed.cpp. No LR algorithm changed.
4. Several reference libraries were not compiled with the caller's exception
   policy. The WASI linker failed on __cxa_allocate_exception/__cxa_throw. CMake
   now consistently disables exceptions for these fixtures. Retained native
   drivers also retain the original no-exceptions policy after their source was
   separated from the shared compiler object target.
5. The full formatter reference scans the Tower source tree through __FILE__.
   The grammar-only interpreter WASI runner could not satisfy that filesystem
   requirement. A trial with Linux Node 22's native node:wasi host terminated with
   exit 139 partway through tests; no root cause is established and that host was
   rejected, consistent with the earlier journal's Windows native-WASI crash.
   `tests/host-wasi.mjs` instead mounts all checked-out Tower fixtures in the
   existing portable TowerWASI host. CMake maps test __FILE__ prefixes to `source`.
   An initial mapping to `.` yielded an empty parent path after filename
   normalization; the explicit `source` mount avoids that ambiguity.
6. Even after mounting fixtures, opendir failed. Instrumenting the actual WASI
   call showed `path_open(..., "source", oflags=2, fdflags=4)` returning NOTSUP
   (58). wasi-libc requests NONBLOCK for directory iteration. The in-memory host
   now accepts APPEND and NONBLOCK (bits 1 and 4), preserves/reports these flags,
   and continues rejecting unsupported synchronization flags. Its files and
   directories are always ready. Added ABI regression coverage to the existing
   JavaScript host test. Worker cancellation/protocol logic is unchanged.

### 2026-11-19 — Host/runtime ownership: first Tower integration checkpoint

Task 4 began by pulling master from 42e2349 to 586078b, then running the
repository-required `git pull --rebase` (already current). Work is isolated on
`port/host-runtime-tower`. The user explicitly requested avoiding new C++:
new policies and functional tests are Tower source; native changes are removal,
temporary ABI/ownership views, seed selection and existing test entry points.
No new C++ source file was added. todo.txt is untouched.

Implemented compiler/host-memory.tower, host-driver.tower, host-text.tower and
host-handles.tower. Production compiler allocation overflow/zero-size policy,
failure injection and allocation observations execute in Tower. CLI option
parsing operates on borrowed argv and caller-supplied link slots, preserving
option order, repeated values, immediate help and existing error text. Browser
response buffers, JSON quoting/unsigned encoding and parser/execution handle
lookup/insertion/removal execute in Tower. The existing worker exports and
transport schema are retained. The shared handle namespace skips zero and live
handles on u32 wrap; destruction takes each payload once. Native SyntaxSession
and CoreMachine payload destructors remain adapters pending their owners' APIs.

Interpreter execution-space bytes now use Tower-owned storage with explicit
growth, zeroing, shrink/regrow and disposal. Failed heap growth preserves the
old bytes, size and heap cursor and returns null; failure to allocate the initial
stack produces a diagnostic. This is execution-space containment, not raw
foundation pointer bounds/lifetime safety. The frozen native interpreter now
uses its existing separate reference declaration, allowing production to drop
its seed-only private methods. Native moves transfer the Tower buffer exactly
once. Its remaining maps, frame/task containers and foreign callbacks have not
yet migrated at this checkpoint.

The bootstrap graph remains honest and acyclic: towerc-seed selects the existing
native allocation/CLI branches with TOWER_BOOTSTRAP_HOST; that seed builds the
Tower host module; stage1 uses the Tower module and the frozen interpreter; the
production hybrid compiler uses the Tower interpreter. Removed unused native
allocation-test policy from the seed branch. This is not a complete Tower-written
compiler, and none of these hybrid executables is being committed as the final
portable bootstrap.

### 2026-11-19 — Interpreter containers and direct Tower entity API

Supersedes the previous checkpoint's native-container limitation: allocation and
free-block maps, string/sequence indexes, per-frame value/address caches, frame
storage and task stacks now live in interpreter-storage.tower. Removed 23 native
container/query entry implementations. These are derived execution indexes over
the existing foundation nodes, not a second semantic model or public encoding.
Maps use sorted u64 entries and binary lower-bound lookup; insertion/erasure move
the contiguous suffix. This replaces std::map allocation overhead but makes
insertion linear in the suffix length; benchmark before claiming a speedup.
Internal cache/container allocation failure retains the previous fatal host
policy via libc abort; guest heap allocation keeps its explicit null result.

CoreMachineState exposes only non-owning ABI views. Tower disposes all arrays;
the remaining native move bridge transfers their pointers once. Added Tower
trials for permuted insertions, updates, absent keys, zero and high-u64 keys,
ordered neighbors, removal, frame-array growth, task LIFO order, cache clearing
and complete disposal. The existing native reference assertions now read the
new views; they still compare complete state at suspension boundaries.

composed with the authoritative entities module. tower.hpp now declares C linkage:
the C++ source signatures and entity layouts are unchanged, but native callers
must rebuild rather than link old mangled names. Native singleton lifetime,
callback registration/finalization and guarded allocation remain in tower.cpp.

## 2026-11-19: Tower template construction, remapping and lexical session traversal

Continued frontend track 1 after `b50bfe0`. This is another migration checkpoint,
not completion of the frontend track or removal of all project-owned C++.

Implemented:

- `compiler/syntax-template.tower` builds typed capture-hole productions directly
  on the existing Rule/Reference/String entities through the Tower emission
  helpers. Scalar tokens use their ordinary generated wrapper; scalar nonterminals
  and repeated/optional captures retain their category/cardinality contracts.
- The same module walks parsed replacement trees iteratively, restores active
  production identities, remaps generated capture labels and counts capture uses.
  It uses the active Tower `LRGrammar` name hash index, replacing a native linear
  name scan for every nonterminal. Sorted borrowed production/alias views remain
  temporary indexes over the existing entities, not an independent grammar model.
- `compiler/syntax-scan.tower` owns source skipping/token traversal, bounded
  diagnostic lookahead, token entity construction, replacement capture recognition,
  identifier decoding and capture lookup. Declaration boundaries and contextual
  tokens still use the existing Tower lexer and parser lookahead. The native
  adapter only borrows session fields, appends highlight records, updates counters
  and passes errors/results to the existing parser-stream interface.
- Replacement names use a borrowed sorted capture array and binary lookup instead
  of a second native capture map. A token's label copies directly into its shared
  Match component, avoiding the old temporary `std::string` substring. Template
  scanning no longer skips the same leading trivia twice.
- Preserved source-relative diagnostic offsets and absolute template-node spans,
  quoted capture identifiers, comments, invalid Unicode-token extent, immutable
  revision inputs, partial-output ownership and the ordinary EOF marker.

The original construction/remapping and scanner code is retained verbatim in
`bootstrap/syntax-template-seed.inc` and `bootstrap/syntax-scan-seed.inc` for the
existing seed/stage1 build only. Production native/Wasm builds run the Tower
implementations. These reference files are still project-owned C++ and must be
deleted when the portable compiler-binary bootstrap replaces the seed. They are
not a permanent bootstrap exception and their relocation is not counted as total
C++ removal. Table/session/revision ownership, diagnostics presentation, native
Bedrock construction, parser stream adapters and remaining frontend tests still
need migration. The other three machines' semantic/backend/host boundaries remain
unchanged.

New functional tests are Tower source:

- `tests/syntax-template.tower` checks scalar/token distinction, the `*`/`+`/`?`
  capture compatibility matrix, rejected literal/unrelated-category helpers,
  generated reference/terminal identities and every injected allocation failure
  until successful construction. Partial grammar roots are disposed and tracked
  allocations must balance on every trial.
- `tests/syntax-scan.tower` checks token labels, spans, rule identity, EOF after a
  token, the full four-byte extent of an unmatched Unicode scalar, and failure
  cleanup at every injected token allocation.
- Public-session replacement fixtures additionally exercise quoted capture names
  and comments on both sides of a capture. Existing parser, replacement,
  formatting, diagnostic and browser tests exercise production integration.

Trials/corrections:

1. Initial template construction/remapping passed the native increment example
   (`5, 6, 7, 7, 9`) and ASan/UBSan CTest 5/5 before scanner work.
2. The new scanner first used `token` as a local name; the current Bedrock reserves
   it for declarations. Renamed the local rather than changing the grammar.
3. The first scanner run used UINT32_MAX for EOF. The existing parser ABI defines
   EOF as UINT32_MAX - 1. This produced the misleading template failure
   "Unexpected end of input. Expected end of input." at a valid final boundary.
   Corrected the marker throughout scanning and added the direct EOF test.
4. Allocation injection exposed a null `entity_release` in scanner cleanup. The
   raw entity API requires a real entity; it is not a null-tolerant smart pointer.
   Guarded cleanup and the test harness's empty-result cleanup explicitly.
   `addr2line -f -C` located the failure in `entity_release` called by
   `syntax_scan_read`; the sanitizer environment's external symbolizer path was
   invalid, so addresses were resolved separately. No API semantics changed.
5. After these fixes, the native increment output again matched exactly and the
   full ASan/UBSan CTest suite passed 5/5 (23.13 seconds on this run). Sanitizers
   instrument the native harness; the generated Tower object is not wholly
   ASan-instrumented. Allocation injection checks Tower-managed storage, not every
   native standard-library allocation.

build/cpp-migration-audit-20261118 worktree before inspection (already current),

Implemented Tower modules already cover entity/component storage, byte/text
utilities, generics specialization, regex/DFA construction, LR analysis/state/
LALR/runtime/control, parser payloads/tree construction, grammar readers and
validation/emission, replacement preparation/expansion, template construction,
token scanning, canonical formatting and interpreter execution/storage. Host
allocation policies, browser handle/text helpers and CLI option parsing/help
also run in Tower. These are production implementations; do not redo them just
because their native references still exist under scaffolding/bootstrap.

Remaining owned native implementation, beyond the pending semantic port:

1. Frontend session/control integration: syntax.cpp still owns Definitions,
   Version and SyntaxSession containers, active/pending rule publication,
   grammar cache lifetime, declaration sequencing, provenance/highlight adapter
   state and user-facing diagnostic selection. parser.cpp still supplies stream
   and recognizer hosts, grammar/table adaptation, conflict presentation and
   repair probing around the Tower LR implementation. bedrock.cpp constructs
   the initial shared grammar entities. compiler-syntax.cpp, syntax-nodes.cpp,
   parser-nodes.cpp and related headers retain registration/access bridges.
   Port these using the existing shared entities, not another authoritative IR.
   The initial Bedrock baseline remains necessary; its constructor can be Tower
   code compiled into the bootstrap binary, so it need not remain C++.
2. Owned backend integration: llvm-engine.cpp still implements Foundation-node
   lowering, verification, pass configuration, target/object emission and
   disassembly. llvm-backend.cpp owns browser linking/results; llvm-wasi.cpp
   supplies owned C++ WASI support overrides. There is no completed Tower backend
   implementation in this merged snapshot. LLVM/lld being third party does not
   exempt our code calling them. Prefer their C interfaces where sufficient;
   resolve C++-only linker/WASI entry points explicitly (native packages can
   bundle an upstream linker executable). Browser support needs its own viable
   binding path; moving our shim under third_party would not finish the port.
3. Host/runtime and residual bridges: driver.cpp still owns filesystem/process
   orchestration and executable linking; browser.cpp owns schema traversal,
   exported session/execution APIs and foreign dispatch. core-machine.cpp,
   tower.cpp, compiler-memory.cpp and format.cpp retain native ownership,
   lifecycle/callback, initialization and host adapters. runtime.c is our own
   guest allocator/startup/platform implementation and must also move. main.cpp
   contains the older native smoke/test entry point. Use explicit Tower host
   contexts and platform interfaces, preserving the browser worker contract.
4. Native tests, bootstrap and build/distribution: functional/reference tests
   remain in C++ and production CMake source lists still compile several of
   them. Translate useful tests to Tower/fixtures before dropping the native
   references. The bootstrap seed can only be removed after a successor can
   build the whole compiler. Historical owned C/C++ research sources also exist
   under docs/research; they are not a production build blocker but need an
   explicit migration/retirement decision for a literal no-owned-C/C++ checkout.

Concrete enabling contracts still missing in this snapshot:

- llvm-engine.cpp rejects exports/externs using tower_allocate/reallocate/
  deallocate/print/trap/main and rejects library top-level executable statements.
  Provide a defined runtime-definition path and explicit initialization entry
  points/state ownership; arbitrary hidden global initialization is not required.
- Semantic builtin lookup prevents directly naming some host functions such as
  realloc/free. Foreign symbol aliases/bindings must distinguish them from Tower
  foundation operations without another native trampoline.
- Native component finalizers, stream callbacks and interpreter foreign dispatch
  still use native callback contracts. Supply typed indirect/foreign calls where
  required, or move internal dispatch to explicit Tower contexts; opaque pointer
  casts alone do not define a callable ABI. Coordinate these requirements with
  the semantic owner rather than overlapping that port.
- Platform startup, I/O and necessary low-level target operations must have
  Tower foundation spellings and explicit ABI/target semantics. Keep deterministic
  compile-time behavior and the same shared entities throughout.

Recommended immediate next work here: complete the frontend session/stream/
diagnostic and Bedrock ownership port, while the other machine completes semantic
analysis. Backend and host integration can proceed against stable shared-node
interfaces in parallel. Measure parser/compile latency, allocations and output

Trials and root causes:

1. Putting lifecycle dispatch in the allocation object made the UTF-8-only test
   link require foundation_node_dispose/compiler_native_finalize. Split lifecycle
   into its own entity-linked object. Utility-only linking now passes.
2. A 64-bit diagnostic guard converted to usize passed native testing but trapped
   on wasm32: Tower numeric conversion checks range, unlike a C++ narrowing cast.
   Select the explicit 32-bit guard before converting. Actual Wasm tests pass.
3. A guest allocator stress assertion found a free tail spanning the cursor:
   first-fit could not combine the free block with unused arena space. Free now
   reclaims a coalesced tail into the cursor, allowing a subsequent 120,000-byte
   request. The test preserves this case and 10,000 deterministic allocation/free
   trials with live-byte validation. This improves the port over runtime.c's old
   full-list coalescing and stranded-tail behavior.
4. Early new tests used a binary expression inside a call, the lexical keyword
   expected as a variable, sizeof(variable), and narrowing convert(u8, index).
   Corrected them to instruction-like locals, ordinary names, explicit types and
   range reduction. No grammar/backend workaround was added.
5. A concurrent browser build briefly executed towerc-stage1 while the native build
   relinked it, producing Permission denied. Finished the native dependency, then
   reran the browser build successfully. Future builds must sequence this dependency.
6. New Tower sources initially failed the repository's canonical formatting check;
   formatted only the owned changed/new Tower files with the existing engine.
   The Wasm execution transport also required the existing declared platform_write
   signature; supplied it explicitly in the test runner instead of allowing imports.

## 2026-11-19: portable fast interpreter, graph profiling, versioned packages

The existing interpreter is a graph interpreter: its Tower task stack evaluates
the checked Foundation entities/components, with entity-keyed value/address maps.
The user requested a second, substantially faster portable interpreter, optimization
of this graph runner, three-way comparison with compiled Wasm, default-enabled UI
targets and, subsequently, versioned `.towerbc` distribution and reconstruction.
That last explicit request supersedes the previous blanket prohibition on binary
distribution containers. AGENTS.md now permits a narrowly defined envelope with
canonical Foundation plus a verified private execution cache. Foundation remains
the authoritative semantic representation; the cache is not an independent IR,
type system, reflection format or public instruction ABI.

Research and choices:

- Lua 5.4's [instruction definitions](https://www.lua.org/source/5.4/lopcodes.h.html)
  illustrate fixed 32-bit instructions and small operand fields with extensions.
  Tower uses an 8-bit operation plus three 8-bit fields in the common case, two
  words for branches and a five-word escape carrying full u32 operands. Explicit
  wide-register/constant/function tests prevent small fields becoming language
  limits. This is a derived cache of Tower operations, not Lua compatibility.
- LLVM's [calling convention contracts](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#calling-conventions)
  explain why pinning an EAX return register or relying on a particular C tail-call
  ABI is not a portable Foundation technique. The runner is ordinary Tower code;
  LLVM chooses registers and dispatch lowering. No guest JIT, executable-memory
  allocation, inline assembly or target-specific trampoline was introduced.
- The [new pass manager](https://llvm.org/docs/NewPassManager.html) optimizes LLVM
  IR. It does not optimize arbitrary bytecode and reconstruct Foundation for us.
  An LLVM-to-cache path would require a verified reconstruction/backend respecting
  types, effects, layouts and strict arithmetic, as implied by the work in
  [writing an LLVM backend](https://llvm.org/docs/WritingAnLLVMBackend.html).
  Today LLVM optimizes the implementation of both interpreters. Guest optimization
  profile 0 preserves the checked Foundation operations; no LLVM guest round trip
  or claim of globally optimal bytecode is implemented.

Implementation:

- `scaffolding/compiler/fast-interpreter.tower` compiles checked nodes into packed
  u32 words, a u64 constant pool and compact out-of-stream function/type/source
  indexes. The hot loop decodes words and accesses contiguous registers. It does
  not walk the graph for ordinary arithmetic, branches, calls or memory access.
  Cold type/string/foreign-call references still belong to the owning program;
  that graph remains alive. The instruction stream contains no compiler metadata
  or graph pointers. Registers reset at statement boundaries; calls reuse frame
  and register capacity. Immutable arrays are trimmed after compilation, and the
  unused graph task/frame/lookup buffers are released when selecting fast mode.
- Both runners share scalar arithmetic, conversion, printing and raw byte-memory
  helpers. Explicit little-endian 1/4/8-byte helpers replace byte-at-a-time loops
  without inheriting host endianness. Graph execution additionally gets a bounded
  256-slot, full-key-checked node lookup cache (4 KiB on a 64-bit host), reusable
  call task/value/address buffers, and stack storage for up to 16 call arguments.
  Larger argument lists still work. Guest allocations and capacity growth can
  allocate; this is not a claim of universally allocation-free interpretation.
- `CoreMachine` selects the Tower runner through a thin host adapter. The native
  production CLI accepts `--interpret-fast`, `--emit bytecode` and `--emit foundation`.
  `.towerbc` input validates and uses its declared pointer layout even when the
  compiler host has a different pointer width. The bootstrap seed does not gain
  a second native interpreter implementation.
- The playground defaults to Graph interpreter, Fast interpreter and WebAssembly,
  plus the detected supported native target. Each can be independently toggled.
  Three separate workers compare outputs/errors, with independent cancellation,
  source editing/restarting and stale-result rejection. Step counts describe each
  runner's internal work and are deliberately not compared for equality.
  Bytecode disassembly displays compilable Foundation loaded from the actual
  downloadable package. A native-only selection still receives Foundation output.
  The Open button continues to import project ZIPs; the CLI and JS host API load
  `.towerbc` files. No new browser file-import flow was added.

Container v1 is defined in `scaffolding/compiler/bytecode-package.tower`, entirely
in Foundation. Its 56-byte header and payload are little endian:

| Offset | Bytes | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 8 | `TOWERBC` followed by NUL |
| 8 / 12 / 16 | 4 each | Container / semantics / execution-cache versions, all 1 |
| 20 | 4 | Explicit target pointer width, 4 or 8 bytes |
| 24 | 4 | Optimization profile, currently 0 |
| 28 / 32 / 36 | 4 each | UTF-8 source byte count / instruction word count / constant count |
| 40 / 44 | 4 each | Total file length / reserved flags (zero) |
| 48 | 8 | FNV-1a-64 checksum, treating these eight bytes as zero |
| 56 onward | variable | Canonical UTF-8 Foundation, then u32 words, then u64 constants |

The loader checks versions, counts, exact bounds, checksum and target profile;
source is capped at 8 MiB and the envelope at 256 MiB. It rebuilds/checks the
Foundation graph and compares every derived instruction/constant before execution.
FNV detects corruption; it is not authentication. Tests modify an instruction and
recompute a valid checksum: cache comparison still rejects the file. Reconstruction
and re-encoding are byte-for-byte deterministic. A package produced in the Wasm
host ran in the Linux native host, reconstructed, and re-encoded identically for
the 32-bit target; both target widths have source/package round-trip coverage.
This v1 design intentionally pays parsing/reconstruction cost and stores source
bytes; it is not a minimal standalone bytecode loader. Future optimizing profiles
must carry the transformed compilable Foundation so disassembly remains semantic.

Profiling, trials and corrections:

- Initial authoring used expressions beyond the instruction-like Foundation and
  aggregate `vector_push`; parser/type errors exposed this. Expanded intermediates
  and used a shared typed reserve/copy helper, then ran the canonical formatter.
- Full differential tests found a foreign callback's supplied error offset being
  replaced by a fast instruction offset. Preserve explicit foreign offsets; resolve
  source runs lazily on interpreter traps. This also removes source-table scans
  from successful calls and loads/stores.
- The first Node `--prof` trial had only 121 ticks and stripped Wasm function names;
  it was unsuitable for attribution. Relinked the same optimized browser object
  files without `--strip-all` and used Node inspector at 100 microseconds, with
  eight executions of 500,000 calls. Final sampled hot functions: graph
  `interpreter_step`, `im_needs`, task pushes, checked node lookups and map reads;
  fast `fast_interpreter_step`, calls and scalar loads/stores. These samples guided
  the changes; they are not instrumented instruction counts or cache-miss counters.
- `llvm-objdump-19 -d` and optimized LLVM inspection of the composed interpreter
  for x86_64 Linux and AArch64 Linux show switch lowering, ordinary branch dispatch,
  masks/shifts (`ubfx` on ARM) and fixed-width loads. This verifies generated code
  shape, not native ARM throughput. Scripts/outputs: `build/fast-x64.ll/.asm` and
  `build/fast-arm64.ll/.asm`; regenerate with production towerc, `--library`, the
  explicit target and `--optimized-ir`, then llvm-objdump. These artifacts are local.
- Early timings overlapped compiler/test builds and are not the final evidence.
  The final idle measurements use three warmups and 15 samples, alternate runner
  order, validate outputs, and separate compile/prepare from execution. Raw samples,
  CPU/Node versions, artifact hashes, capacities and aggregated profiles are checked
  in at `docs/research/2026-11-19-interpreters.json`.

Final median execution times (ms), AMD Ryzen AI MAX+ 395, Windows Node 21.7.3 Wasm
host; native measurements use Linux x64 in Docker, Node 22.23.5, LLVM/Clang 19:

| Workload | Previous graph | Improved graph | Fast | Compiled Wasm | Native graph | Native fast |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| arithmetic | 5.178 | 3.601 | 0.962 | 0.367 | 1.498 | 0.566 |
| calls | 3.723 | 2.630 | 0.607 | 0.244 | 1.054 | 0.365 |
| memory | 7.155 | 4.887 | 1.683 | 0.276 | 2.310 | 1.270 |
| branch | 7.096 | 4.996 | 1.285 | 0.350 | 2.169 | 0.800 |

Graph execution decreases 29-32%; fast is 2.90-4.33x the improved graph in the Wasm
host and 1.82-2.89x in native Linux. Compiled Wasm remains faster for all four.
Wasm execution timing includes module compilation/instantiation and invocation;
LLVM guest compilation is separately recorded. It is not an isolated Wasm CPU
throughput measurement. Baseline is the previously deployed graph reactor, SHA-256
`0aeb6dda968bb18e07611f8c58beda239483642a6462e6e8c36813d73e4c21f3`, from the
preceding runtime release (same runtime at starting main 6610461).
Packed code is 156/196/236/216 bytes; measured cache capacities after running are
516/856/636/608 bytes respectively. These exclude the retained Foundation graph,
host adapters and shared 4 MiB guest arena. Packaging source increases file size.
The runner is compact and contiguous, not a zero-memory-overhead claim.

Reproduce from the repository root (after the documented production/browser builds):

```text
TOWER_BENCH_BASELINE=build/fast-baseline.wasm node playground/scripts/benchmark-interpreters.mjs report.json
node scaffolding/tests/benchmark-interpreters.mjs /path/to/towerc native-report.json
TOWER_PROFILE_REACTOR=build/fast-profile.wasm node playground/scripts/profile-interpreters.mjs
npm test --prefix playground
npm run check:format --prefix playground
npm run test:browser --prefix playground
npm run test:deployment --prefix playground
TOWER_NATIVE_BUILD=/cache/shared-native bash playground/scripts/test-bootstrap.sh
```

first. Native build/test caches live in Docker volume `tower_host_cache`; source is
mounted at `/work`. Browser WASI SDK is 34, wasm32 p1. ASan/UBSan instruments the
native host/harness, not the separately LLVM-emitted Tower instructions.

## 2026-11-19 — Tower/Wasm completion and shared browser highlighting

Request: make browser typing offer useful suggestions, keep the engine in Tower
and on the shared entity/component hierarchy, and fix the source/instructions
highlighting mismatch shown in the increment example.

Implemented `compiler/completion.tower` in the existing semantic compiler object.
The query follows the ordinary parse entities' ordered children, named captures,
ParserMatch components and parent hierarchy. Its candidate lists contain borrowed
entity handles; there is no independent JS symbol table or serialized completion
IR. Built-in names and scalar spellings come from `semantic-definitions.tower`.
The current implementation handles visible locals/parameters, module-wide forward
functions/structs/variables, globals from other project files, explicit receiver
struct fields, type positions, active grammar references and keywords. Locals
shadow globals even when a module declaration occurs later in the source.

Rejected a separate text-scanning symbol database: it would diverge from custom
Tower grammar and the compiler's scopes. Instead, the shared lexer locates the
completion range and unfinished statement; recovery blanks that statement without
shifting existing coordinates, closes bounded missing braces, then invokes the
ordinary parser. Thus recovered locals still come from shared parser entities.
Recovery is disposable query input, never saved source or an executable program.
It does not run user code. Earlier unrelated parse errors, inferred receiver
types, member chains and generic specialization remain limitations; this is not
full semantic type-directed completion. Future work should query available checked
FoundationType/binding components and extend shared parser recovery, rather than
add another type checker or symbol model.

The small C++ browser/session adapter still orchestrates the current bootstrap
parser and borrows grammar projections. Query decisions, recovery construction,
entity traversal, scope filtering, prefix matching, deduplication and JSON
construction run in Tower compiled to Wasm. Full removal of that native adapter
belongs to the existing compiler migration. JS converts UTF-16/UTF-8 offsets and
handles CodeMirror, workers, request coalescing and stale-result rejection. The
popup opens on typing or Ctrl+Space; arrows navigate, Tab/Enter or click/touch
accept, Escape dismisses, and normal Tab indentation works when no popup is open.
Completion has an independent worker and 100 ms activation delay; analysis and
execution retain their 200 ms trailing debounce. Workers terminate at ten seconds.

Highlighting root cause: `output-syntax.mjs` maintained an independent Tower keyword
list and classified names/types differently from the source lexer. Removed that
Tower path. Source, canonical instructions and reconstructed Foundation now share
`syntax_get_highlights` and one CodeMirror decoration engine. Generated Foundation
uses the bundled canonical grammar; LLVM/machine displays retain their separate
lexers. Highlight requests coalesce per output, cache only a bounded set of texts,
and reject responses for replaced documents. The increment regression compares
actual identifier/keyword classes and computed colors across all three Tower panes.

Tooling now receives lexical classification separately from `as style`, including
unstyled skip spans. String/comment suppression must not break when Identifier is
styled as string/pattern or String is styled as identifier. The private token index
is resolved back to shared declaration metadata for GrammarPattern; it is not a
persisted semantic identity. Presentation snapshots still omit unstyled spans.

## 2026-11-19 — Tower language roadmap before implementation

Read AGENTS.md and pulled/rebased main (already current at c6815f5). The requested
language direction is recorded in docs/tower-language-plan.md before code work:
file-identity namespaces and selective imports; dependency-query resolution;
nominal enums; match; C#-like expression grouping and exact overloads; deterministic
graph-interpreter staging with capability/file dependencies; move/borrow/drop,
universal iterators and containers; properties/constraints/reflection; eval and
typed attributes. New implementation and functional tests will be Tower only.

The first bounded slice is match/while control flow and generic collection
basics. Existing replacements lack hygiene, so match must lower to bound shared
Foundation entities rather than textual temporaries. Nominal enums are sequenced
after a serializable type-identity contract; integer aliases will not be sold as
enums. Automatic dereference is a member-access convenience, not memory safety;
automatic address-taking must wait for place/borrow rules. Associativity controls
parse grouping and is separate from algebraic reassociation/commutativity.

Sources reviewed: the journal's replacement/hygiene, operand effect-order,
template and import entries; semantic-{context,types,values,statements}.tower;
the existing generic vector. C# specification and Rust match reference URLs are
in the plan. This supersedes no existing arithmetic, effect or Foundation storage
contract. No enums/comptime/general expression implementation is claimed by the
plan. todo.txt remains untouched.

### Error-model steering during the first language slice

The user requires Rust-style returned errors with very little syntax and then
made both exclusions absolute: no GC and no exceptions. Added a dedicated design
section to docs/tower-language-plan.md: ordinary tagged result(T, E)/option(T),
exhaustive match, and eventual `try` propagation as branches/returns. Exact error
types, active-payload ownership, aggregate return and early-return cleanup must
exist before sugar. No throw/catch/unwind or GC runtime is being introduced.
Current vector/stack/queue APIs use boolean results plus preserved output
parameters. Result types and propagation are planned, not claimed implemented.

### First language slice: implementation and validation

Implemented TowerMatch/TowerWhile grammar in scaffolding/tower.tower and lowering
in compiler/semantic-control.tower. Foundation syntax and its operation ABI remain
unchanged. The same surface entities acquire Foundation components; generated
locals/blocks/comparisons/branches are ordinary shared entities, bound directly.
Match supports integer/bool literals, alternatives, a required final wildcard,
duplicate/range diagnostics, one subject evaluation, scopes and outer-loop
break/continue. While requires a bool condition and braces. All paths serialize
to compilable Foundation; lowering accounts for its existing nesting limit.
These are statement forms, not general expressions or full pattern matching.

Collection implementation is Tower: vector_pop/vector_move, stack(T) as a vector
policy, and queue(T) as a growing FIFO ring. Empty/null-output/oversized-reserve
failure preserves state/output; successful moves replace initialized destination
storage and reset the source, including self-move handling. Scalar/pointer element
support is explicit; no automatic aggregate copy/drop or pointee destruction.
The compiler completion traversal now uses vector_pop. The playground includes
Match and Collections examples, and imports expose/remove the actual stack,
vector and queue files in the builtin tree. JavaScript edits are existing web
transport/test/formatter adapters; all language algorithms and behavioral fixture
assertions are Tower. No C/C++ source or build recipe changed.

Trials and corrections:

  derived spelling index; bindings remain entity references, not name guesses.
- A while-true return initially hid the literal behind a local, so reparsing its
  canonical Foundation would lose definite-return knowledge. Literal conditions
  now remain visible; added always_returns() to the Tower fixture and tested the
  canonical result. Other conditions use a local evaluated per loop iteration.
- Added lowered-depth accounting rather than accepting matches whose emitted
  nested branches exceed Foundation's limit. No arbitrary limit was removed.
- Existing `expected` and `token` grammar keywords caught two new local names;
  changed them to descriptive ordinary identifiers. Compiler/bootstrap errors
  were resolved in Tower, with no new seed behavior.
- Source formatting lacked builtin-library inputs for examples importing
