The user's follow-up strengthens this direction: automatic specialization should
aggressively exploit fixed data, without requiring explicit user code generation.
Treat this as part of the compile-time compiler design. Eligible ordinary Tower
code should expose constants through calls and immutable aggregates, inline and
fold known control flow, unroll statically bounded loops when profitable, and
specialize a generic fixed-DFA runner into state-specific code when justified.
An unknown-length input still requires repetition, and input characters still
select runtime transitions. Absence of callbacks/dynamic dispatch does not make
those values compile-time constants. No unconditional full-unrolling or perfect
assembly guarantee is valid; recursive/cyclic state graphs need finite code and
code-size/work budgets. Preserve effects, numeric/target contracts and canonical
Foundation provenance; use reference/differential tests and inspect generated code
plus throughput/code size. Manual staged code generation remains useful, but is
not the prerequisite users should need for this case. ECS/threading and lazy
dependency execution remain the immediate prerequisites and current priority;
parser/JSON benchmarking has not been started.

A further explicit correction from the user supersedes the earlier description
of a separate inferred-constant propagation optimization: do not introduce a
special pre-LLVM constant-folding/propagation pass. Known values must come from
generic execution of ordinary Foundation operations through the shared Tower
interpreter, including literal values. Input/dependency/effect tracking determines
when execution is possible; the interpreter produces results. Optimized shortcuts,
execution caches and future native execution tiers must implement that same
contract, not an independent evaluator or algebraic folding rule set. No separate
constant-propagation pass was implemented during this discussion. LLVM's own
optimization pipeline is a separate backend concern.

EntityStage now supports coordinator-granted exclusive attachment leases over
existing source entities. Workers may add stable canonical component payloads to
their own owners without changing global typed indexes, type references or store
counts. Publication reserves capacity before updating those indexes after joins;
discard frees only the newly attached components. This is not rollback of arbitrary
existing payload writes and does not permit concurrent readers of a leased owner's
mutable component list. The scheduler must grant exclusive owner/payload access.

ownership cleanup alongside the existing independent-world invocation tests.

entities; results and first diagnostics publish in source order. Layout reads use

ordinary result components on the worker, then enter the dependency scheduler at

### 2026-11-20 - ECS LALR action ranges

Implemented an LRAction kernel in Tower using the existing shared compiler
kernel dispatcher. Split the ordinary LALR algorithm at solved lookahead and
reuse one ordered per-state action builder for serial and worker execution.
The closure pool remains alive across the boundary. After closing the closure
view, reset its fully joined WorkGraph with a new revision, attach transient
range-job components, declare immutable input/disjoint result ranges, then pin
and dispatch. Workers own private vectors; successful joins publish them in
state order. Failure drains admitted work before releasing inputs or outputs
and does not publish partial action tables. Grammar nodes remain authoritative;
these tables and task indexes are derived analysis data. Use at least 128 states
per task as an initial batching policy, not a measured speedup guarantee.

Expanded the conflicting/nullable-cycle Tower LR fixture with a 256-terminal
prefix so its action stage crosses the parallel threshold. Every item, transition,

### 2026-11-20 - Lookahead fixed-point worker continuation

The next working-tree slice splits propagation graph construction from solving.
For a wide frontier, group changed source contributions by unique destination,
then dispatch ECS range jobs through the existing closure/action pool and shared
WorkGraph. Each job clones its destination's prior ranges into a private buffer
and invokes the ordinary range-merge routines over immutable source ranges.
Join all jobs, publish changed destinations in deterministic frontier order,
then enqueue the next frontier. Reuse vector capacity across waves and reset
work receipts with a new revision only after joining. Narrow frontiers use the
existing serial worklist. This is ordinary parser fixed-point evaluation, not a
constant-folding pass or parser specialization/code generation.

Legal grammar cycles converge monotonically; dependency cycles in compile-time
queries remain errors under the separate existing query contract. The new Tower
fixture compares all ranges/queue flags with serial results for 128 seeded cyclic
lanes, duplicate/self/diamond edges, overlapping ranges and one empty cycle.
It also requires multiple admitted jobs and multiple joined revisions when more
than one worker is available, alongside the existing real-overlap pool fixture.

and structural semantic continuation work remain outstanding. No C++ introduced.

operand of a decltype query. It borrows the existing canonical type without

retain ordinary value restrictions; a blanket aggregate allowance whenever

operators. The query root is private checking context, restored at nested query
boundaries. No evaluator, propagation pass, C++ implementation or aggregate
copy/call/return semantics were added.

### 2026-11-20 - Root-block checking continuation and structural body receipts

Block checking now shares begin/step/finish operations and a private cursor for
source position, flow, label state and cleanup boundary. Function checking uses
that same path. A function with a structural prefix and an independent remaining
suffix can preserve its lexical scopes on the function's ECS work component,
finish interning/layout publication on the coordinator, and resume ordinary
checking under a worker lease. No statement or operand is speculatively retried.
Prefix scope allocations remain compilation-owned; worker scratch remains private;
flow dependencies and captured cleanup bindings transfer at the join. Clear
borrowed context pointers on failed preparation as well as successful publication.

Structural prefixes now have BodyPrepareQuery receipts. Their suffix BodyQuery
explicitly depends on preparation and completed layouts. Entire structural bodies
also use BodyQuery tickets. Access claims distinguish the owned body range and
shared interning/index state. These coordinator jobs still execute synchronously
at a join boundary: being represented in the graph is not itself threading.
Nested structural blocks, arbitrary operand suspension and parallel interning
remain unimplemented. Admission currently finishes earlier bodies before preparing
a later structural prefix, preserving diagnostic and construction order but
limiting useful batch sizes when adjacent functions both need preparation.

### 2026-11-20 - Stable component pages and worker allocation ownership

Reviewed the original stable-sparse ECS rationale, the pinned-query limitations,
and stage/lease publication contracts above, plus library/entities.tower and
entity_stage.tower. Native entity/component interfaces use opaque pointers; their
payload addresses must remain stable, including legacy nontrivial native payloads.
Current type indexes are dense pointers to individual allocations. Do not call
that archetype or packed payload storage.

Next implementation: pack small same-type payloads into stable pages, preserving
all public entity/component access and lifetime contracts. Coordinator allocation
uses a store-local pool; each worker stage uses its own pool, including additions
to leased entities. Full pages detach from allocation pools, and publication
releases stage pool ownership without moving payloads. Last-component cleanup
reclaims its page. Large/over-aligned payloads retain individual allocation.
Pool keys use store-local monotonic type IDs, not reusable allocation addresses.
No worker changes shared pool state or type indexes. This is a storage-density
step with holes after removal, not relocating multi-component archetypes or a
SIMD/speed guarantee. Implementation and fault/lifetime/parallel tests are next;
this paragraph records the design, not verified support.

Small-component pages are implemented in Tower with a 16 KiB slot budget and
at most 64 rows. Each page stores a contiguous header range and a strided aligned
payload range; payloads keep the existing back-reference/access contract and are
not implicitly zeroed. Oversized/aligned rows fall back to individual allocation.
Partial pages unlink on last-component destruction, full pages stop being
allocation candidates, and stage publication detaches all remaining private pool
links before freeing the stage. No page retains a type pointer as a reusable key.
Stage creation/leases install an explicit private pool on the entity; a missing
pool on a staged owner fails instead of falling back to shared mutation.

The first entity_pages fixture passes with output 0 in graph/fast interpreters at
both pointer widths, using the preceding compiler to run the new Tower library.
It covers multiple pages, 64-byte alignment, stable survivors after removals,
re-addition, large sparse allocation, overflow rejection, separate stage pools,
pinned publication rejection, deterministic reverse stage publication, leased
node additions, discard and complete store cleanup. Integrated production storage
builds, actual worker overlap and native allocator/lifetime coverage are running.
No new native code. This is packed stable per-type storage with holes, not full
multi-component archetypes or measured faster execution.

### 2026-11-20 - Remaining Flecs-style storage/query contract

Reviewed upstream Flecs docs at commit
85188ed19f971c201af61c26143fa69877fe418b (2026-11-20), through the public GitHub
connector. Primary references:
[component traits](https://github.com/SanderMertens/flecs/blob/85188ed19f971c201af61c26143fa69877fe418b/docs/ComponentTraits.md),
[queries](https://github.com/SanderMertens/flecs/blob/85188ed19f971c201af61c26143fa69877fe418b/docs/Queries.md),
[systems](https://github.com/SanderMertens/flecs/blob/85188ed19f971c201af61c26143fa69877fe418b/docs/Systems.md).

Flecs groups equal component sets into tables and can cache matching tables.
Sparse storage preserves addresses through table transitions; non-fragmenting
traits can additionally avoid splitting tables for infrequent metadata. These
are separate choices. Its staging model protects iteration while structural
changes accumulate, and multithreaded systems partition matched table ranges.
Access declarations inform synchronization. The relevant target is compiler-wide
shared entities/components, archetype-aware queries and dependency/access-aware
worker scheduling, while preserving required ordering; not a claim that every
operation executes simultaneously.

Tower's new pages preserve its existing stable-payload contract. Next: archetype
membership and multi-component query ranges/cache invalidation, with explicit
stable versus relocatable storage policies. Existing compiler pointers cannot
silently become movable column borrows. Stages must prepare all fallible table
reservations before publishing canonical membership; failed publication preserves
identities/query lengths. Queries under pins must use published indexes/columns,
not another worker's leased mutable component list. Sparse query metadata must
not accidentally multiply archetypes without an explicit policy. Source-order
publication and stale revision/profile tickets remain required. These are next
implementation constraints, not completed archetype/query features.

### 2026-11-21 - Archetype membership and pinned multi-component plans

Integrated the isolated exact-signature table implementation into the Tower
entity store. Every published nonempty entity has one derived table row, with
sorted monotonic type IDs, dense entity rows and columns of stable component
pointers. Component add/remove and stage publication reserve before committing;
reclamation does not allocate. Pending destination counts prevent an empty table
from being freed while another prepared row still targets it. Failed stage
preparation cancels every reservation while preserving canonical membership and
published query lengths. Types and metadata stay ordinary entities/components.

AND queries cache matched tables and column mappings inside EntityView. The view
owns/frees its plans; plans cannot survive structural unpinning. Workers borrow
immutable table ranges and private cursors, without reading another worker's
mutable leased component list. These are stable sparse payload columns, not
relocating packed component data. Empty entities are not indexed, and a query
requires at least one distinct registered component term from the same world.

Integrated worker-private names and queued payload reference ownership into the
existing EntityStage. Publication validates name collisions and reserves all
storage before committing; existing members are not silently replaced. Names
transfer into ordinary containment. The worker queues references to immutable
published entities without updating shared counts. After joins, the coordinator
holds queued ownership before the last input view closes; a held cursor prevents
repeat retains on publication retries. Discard holds before ordinary payload
finalizers, balancing successfully installed private ownership. Caller scheduling
must preserve input lifetimes and prevent leasing queued reference targets.

The formatted body-continuation draft is now integrated. One ECS body-work
component owns its source boundaries, persistent block cursor and lexical state;
BodyQuery suspends on construction receipts keyed by the next syntax child, then
returns to the ordinary Tower worker kernel. Worker-created lexical allocations
and lists transfer to compilation ownership after joining. Every stage in a batch
publishes before coordinator metadata writes or structural preparation. Checked
statements are never replayed. Error publication waits for earlier source bodies,
including across multiple suspensions; unfinished later work is reclaimed after
an earlier error. Editor/type-use observation and malformed-body diagnostics keep
the coordinator path; failed observation clears the work component's borrowed
context. Nested structural statements still require nested continuations.

A further header_bodies_draft removes the whole-if preparation restriction.
Immutable boundary records distinguish a structural condition from a whole leaf
statement. Its existing BodyPrepareQuery enters the shared if header exactly once,
opens the branch cursor and publishes any new layouts; the suspended body then
resumes that branch on a worker. Branch contents never replay the condition.
The same sem_body_enter helper serves worker and coordinator entry. Boundary
records and cursors remain derived scheduling data on the existing ECS work

Shipped implementation at 6fcad397a10797b879011755a838e8a9c916779f:

1. Unevaluated decltype and interpreter-backed scalar comptime, including forward
   declarations/signatures/fields, nested demanded stages, cycle diagnostics,
   strict initialized/live local reads, fuel and explicit target data. Ordinary
   runtime and stage execution share operation semantics. General aggregate/type
   values, heap/file/network capabilities and inferred execution are not included.
2. Shared ECS dependency suspension/yield, fresh dispatch tickets, stale-result
   rejection, failure/cancellation handling and declared access ranges. Layout,
   evaluation, declaration and body preparation use this machinery. Graphs remain
   per-compilation; this is not persistent incremental dependency caching.
3. Real bounded native Linux and shared-memory Wasm worker execution, portable
   fallback, joined publication and deterministic diagnostics. Windows/macOS
   transports were object-compiled; execution on those hosts has not been verified.
4. Stable component payload pages, exact-signature archetype membership, published
   component pointer columns and pinned cached multi-component queries. Syntax,
   grammar and Foundation use the shared entity lookup; worker stages create
   canonical entities and carry explicit leases. These are not relocated packed
   SoA payloads, and table membership alone does not make every compiler path safe.
5. Parallel layout, declaration discovery/readiness and eligible declaration type
   checking, including fields, signatures, operators, calls and generic deduction.
   Generic signatures no longer force unused bodies; demanded generic bodies are
   cloned and checked through worker queries. Type interning/construction still
   has coordinator work.
6. Ordinary body checking/lowering and staged flow checks on workers. Persistent
   lexical/control cursors resume across construction dependencies through nested
   blocks, if/else and Foundation loops without replaying earlier statements.
   Surface handlers and individual structural expressions are not all converted.
7. Worker kernels for FIRST/nullable, LR state/kernel closures, LALR dependency
   links, lookahead propagation, actions and runtime table rows. Shared interning,
   graph/result merging and grammar activation retain ordered publication.
8. Explicit compiler worlds for module/syntax/execution sessions and native CLI
   requests; callable native multi-unit compiler services with exclusive worlds
   and bounded nested workers. Mixed compile/editor-inspection units run through
   ECS jobs. This is not finished native CLI project orchestration or internally

9. AGENTS.md contribution rules for the shared graph, ownership/access, dependency

Why time accumulated and process correction:

The underlying work crossed several mutable ownership boundaries, not one pool
addition. Real blockers included shared-Wasm memory growth/failure delivery,
legacy allocation-counter races between units, worker transport oversubscription,
implicit generic/protocol construction under pinned reads, and preserving lexical,
defer and error order across suspended bodies. Concurrent upstream language and
bootstrap changes also required integration and rebuilt validation.

There was avoidable overhead too: too many small full release cycles, repeated
validation of near-adjacent drafts, harness/import/formatting mistakes, and builds
competing with browser verification before the quiet-verifier rule. Existing
performance work even had to correct excessively fine worker dispatch. The records
do not permit an honest percentage breakdown of elapsed time. A clear end-to-end
completion ledger should have been maintained and surfaced sooner, instead of
letting checkpoint detail stand in for an answer about the overall endpoint.
Batch related implementation before release, retain focused ownership/differential
checks, and reserve full successor/browser/deployment runs for coherent milestones.

Completion means all independent eligible compiler work has explicit ECS ownership
and dependency scheduling, with required source/effect order and structural commits
represented by deliberate barriers. It does not mean eliminating synchronization.
There are still substantial workstreams, so no defensible "almost 100%" or universal
Flecs/threading completion claim follows from the shipped milestones.

### 2026-11-21 — ECS compiler architecture assessment

The user asked whether universal ECS/archetypes plus threading is objectively a
sound compiler design, particularly for dependency chains. Checked primary docs:
https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/query.html describes memoized, demand-driven
queries and dynamically discovered dependencies. Its parallel-rustc page explicitly
warns that historical implementation/default-status details are outdated, so do
not use it to assert current shipping defaults. MLIR's operation-pass restrictions
(https://mlir.llvm.org/docs/PassManagement/) isolate mutation and prohibit shared
mutable pass globals. Flecs documents row slicing and staged structural publication
(https://www.flecs.dev/flecs/Systems.html#threading). LLVM ORC documents context locks
and separate contexts for increased compilation concurrency
(https://llvm.org/docs/ORCv2.html#how-to-use-threadsafemodule-and-threadsafecontext).

Assessment: shared entities/ownership, batched component queries and demand-driven
ready-task scheduling are a sound combination. Flecs storage/pipelines alone do
not discover semantic dependencies. Ready tasks should come from across the graph;
a suspended query releases its worker rather than owning a thread for its whole
chain. Shared producers should deduplicate, and genuine dependency chains still
bound parallelism. Tiny tasks, unnecessary structural transitions, pointer chasing,
shared interning and overbroad barriers can outweigh threading benefits. Universal
semantic identity does not require one dispatch per AST operation or packed payload
relocation everywhere. Keep profitable batching and stable payloads where needed.
These are design judgments, not measured whole-compiler speedup claims. Measure
elapsed time/scaling as well as utilization; busy cores can be doing redundant work.

The integrated while/for fast path passes (surface-integrated-smoke.log). Shared
begin/finish phases for deferred block registration and foreach protocol setup
are now implemented locally, with cursors on SemanticBodyWork. Foreach preparation
still constructs its implicit protocol on the coordinator; its body can suspend
and resume on workers. Deferred block scopes retain their capture/loop/local-frame
state across those same boundaries. Resumed iteration completion explicitly leases
its retained generated iteration block. Initial existing-fixture smoke passes
(iteration-defer-smoke.log). Added a typed-parameter foreach fixture with generic
calls, nested deferred captures, continue and break; its focused run is underway.
No claim of publication or complete structural-expression/type-construction work.

### 2026-11-21 — Stronghold: a future safe language above Tower

The user asks whether the ECS/threading work could support Stronghold above
tower.tower: no raw pointers or unsafe operations in application code, initialized
values, safe ECS access, type-directed race prevention, and possibly an optional
mode permitting races whose outcomes remain memory-safe. This entry is a design
proposal, not implemented language behavior and not a change of the current
compiler ECS/compile-time priority. All future project-owned implementation belongs
in Tower. No Stronghold implementation is introduced by this entry.

Existing intent and current foundation:

No occurrence of Stronghold was found in the tracked project before this entry.
Related ideas are already in todo.txt: around lines 3680–3745, weak parent handles,
nullable access after deletion, alternative ownership models and a less restrictive
feel than Rust; around 7555–7580, deferred tree changes/destruction while readers
exist and safety added above the core; around 8856, explicitly building a C-like
unsafe core with a safe layer on top. Other older notes discuss initialization,
checked regions and pointer restrictions. todo.txt remains untouched. These are
historical ideas, not evidence that their guarantees are implemented.

Stronghold fits the present architecture. Tower foundation keeps raw target
pointers and its explicit low-level semantics. Stronghold can supply surface rules,
safe libraries, types and enforced semantic restrictions on the same entities and
operations. Its lowering still has compilable foundation spellings and uses the
same interpreter and backend path. It needs no separate public graph, instruction
ABI or constant evaluator. Safe handles are additional abstractions, not a change
back to the retired checked-foundation-pointer prototype.

The boundary must be semantic:

Removing pointer syntax from a grammar would be useful presentation, but would
not enforce safety. Imports, replacements, reflection, compile-time code generation
and foreign calls could otherwise recreate unchecked access. A Stronghold compile
profile must check the expanded program and transitive calls, including generated
code, before accepting it. Safe modules cannot forge handles, reinterpret bytes as
references, perform unchecked address arithmetic, free borrowed storage, expose
uninitialized values or invoke arbitrary unsafe Tower functions. Reflection must
respect the same ownership and access capabilities as ordinary code.

Implementations of safe containers and the scheduler may internally use raw
foundation operations behind a small, explicit trusted boundary. Trust must be
assigned by build/module policy, never by a user-forgeable annotation or a favorable
function name. Public interfaces must protect their invariants even for hostile
but well-typed callers. Foreign/native functions need trusted wrappers and effect,
lifetime and threading contracts. Ordinary Stronghold modules need no unsafe
escape hatch; explicitly trusted Tower modules are a distinct boundary. A safety
claim depends on the compiler/runtime and those wrappers being correct, as it does
for other safe languages. A Wasm sandbox alone does not protect one guest object
from corruption by another object in the same linear memory.

Keep memory safety, valid typed values, race freedom and determinism distinct.
Preventing a dangling access does not guarantee the right entity was selected;
preventing a data race does not establish a deterministic order of independent
effects; and a valid integer can still encode a wrong application result.

Handles, access and reclamation:

- Persistent references should be opaque typed handles with a world identity,
  slot and incarnation, or an equivalent non-forgeable identity scheme. Lookup
  checks world, liveness, component presence and type. Wrong-world access and
  stale IDs cannot accidentally resolve to an unrelated object. Component removal
  needs an explicit contract too: an entity lookup asks for its current component,
  while a handle to a particular component incarnation must not silently rebind
  after remove/re-add. Persistent serialization needs explicit identity remapping.
- A stale weak handle can produce an absent result. Slot-generation wrap must have
  a real policy, such as retiring the slot before reuse would alias a live old
  handle; being statistically unlikely is insufficient for a guarantee. World
  destruction and world-ID reuse need equivalent protection. Bevy's Entity docs
  explicitly distinguish an ID from an existing entity and warn about eventual
  ID aliasing; this is a useful limit to account for rather than copy blindly.
  [Bevy Entity](https://docs.rs/bevy_ecs/latest/bevy_ecs/entity/struct.Entity.html).
- Checking the generation and then returning an unprotected address is unsound:
  another job could destroy or relocate the component between the check and use.
  Lookup must acquire protected access as part of one protocol. A successful
  borrow remains valid for its entire permitted scope. It cannot spontaneously
  become a dangling reference halfway through an expression.
- Begin with scoped world/query views, exclusive mutation rights and staged
  structural changes after readers join. Archetype movement, sparse component
  removal, buffer growth, compaction and destruction all obey this rule. Stable
  payload addresses simplify relocation but do not solve concurrent destruction.
  If later measurements justify more overlap, locks, protected immutable snapshots,
  hazard pointers or epoch reclamation are implementation choices. Crossbeam's
  epoch documentation illustrates delayed destruction while readers are pinned;
  a lifetime pin still does not grant permission to race on mutable payload data.
  [Crossbeam epoch](https://docs.rs/crossbeam-epoch/latest/crossbeam_epoch/).
- Persist handles or owned snapshots across job boundaries and suspension. A
  short-lived component borrow cannot escape into a closure, global, suspended
  continuation or another worker unless its type carries a supported lifetime and
  access transfer. Reacquire access after resumption. Cancellation must release
  borrows only after work drains; a cancelled task cannot leave a reader using
  reclaimed memory. Bound long-lived pins so they do not indefinitely retain
  entire worlds. Reentrant callbacks must follow these rules too.

Typed ECS access and threading:

Give queries and functions read, write, structural-mutation and effect requirements.
Infer access through calls where possible and check declared contracts elsewhere.
The scheduler can run compatible readers and disjoint writers concurrently;
conflicting mutation requires ordering or exclusive access. Component type alone
may be a conservative first access set. Proven entity ranges, partitions and query
filters can later recover parallelism without weakening safety. Two parameters
that may refer to the same entity still need an alias check or proof.

Dynamic entity lookup is common in games and compiler graphs. It should remain
usable through a checked borrow, safe synchronized operation, snapshot or exclusive
context when a static proof is unavailable. An arbitrary callback cannot silently
access data outside the system's declared capabilities. Custom query providers
cannot lie about access. Bevy's SystemParam safety contract likewise requires
complete access registration and conflict prevention; this supports the proposed
direction, not a claim that Tower already implements equivalent enforcement.
[Bevy SystemParam](https://docs.rs/bevy_ecs/latest/bevy_ecs/system/trait.SystemParam.html#safety).

Dependency scheduling and access scheduling solve different constraints. A ready
job still needs its data capabilities; a conflict-free job still waits for required
results. Do not block workers while holding access that a dependency needs. For
deterministic mode, publication and conflicting effects also require a specified
order. Stronghold need not make every scalar or temporary an ECS entity: ordinary
stack values, pure functions and uniquely owned containers remain useful. ECS is
particularly attractive for shared world data, graph identity and coarse access
lifetimes, where it can make the safe path convenient.

Initialization, ownership and ordinary collections:

Every observable value must be initialized and valid for its type. Require an
initializer or a type-defined valid default, and check definite assignment before
reads. Zeroed bytes are not automatically a valid non-null reference, enum,
resource or invariant-bearing struct. Tower's existing zero/default mechanism is
not by itself the Stronghold contract. Partially built objects stay private until
complete; failed construction must neither publish invalid fields nor destroy
fields that never acquired ownership. Define cleanup on ordinary returns, errors,
cancellation and traps instead of assuming existing defer implies unwinding.

Safe arrays and slices expose only their initialized length, preserve valid tags
and reference representations, and check bounds and layout/address arithmetic.
Allocator capacity is not initialized content. Growth cannot invalidate a live
borrow. Static proofs may remove checks; otherwise checks remain in release builds.
Older suggestions that release mode simply removes required safety checks do not
fit Stronghold. This is language enforcement, not a request for sanitizer sweeps.

World/arena ownership plus weak entity handles can avoid a mandatory tracing GC.
Unique values and moves can cover local resources, with shared ownership only
where useful. Reference counting is an optional technique, not an automatic cure
for cycles. Define cycle/resource-leak policy separately; memory safety alone
does not guarantee bounded memory consumption or prompt destruction. Avoid making
every component access update a global reference count. Scoped query access can
amortize checks over a whole batch, preserving dense traversal. Actual overhead
must be measured; neither zero cost nor a fixed percentage loss is established.

What the optional race-permitting mode could mean:

Keep memory safety and type validity mandatory in every Stronghold profile.
Relax only ordering/consistency requirements through defined operations. A useful
default rejects or orders conflicting ordinary accesses. Optional shared cells,
snapshots or concurrent collections could allow a well-defined old/new value,
an absent entity, or an explicit update conflict. Lost updates may be an accepted
logical race for a particular operation, but corruption and fabricated references
are never accepted outcomes. This does not need to expose hardware data races.

For example, if deletion wins before a weak lookup acquires access, lookup returns
absent. If acquisition wins, the reader retains valid storage until release and
deletion waits or retires the old storage. A conflicting write might serialize,
use compare/exchange, reduce values, or report failure. Specify each operation's
ordering and failure semantics rather than silently discarding writes or promising
that every kind of race can somehow be converted to null.

Compound values require particular care: independently atomic pointer and length
fields can still form an invalid pair. Publish a protected immutable record,
lock the record or use another protocol preserving the whole invariant. Go's memory
model explicitly warns that racing multiword pointer/length or pointer/type pairs
can cause memory corruption; it is a concrete counterexample to assuming ordinary
typed access automatically makes races harmless.
[Go memory model](https://go.dev/ref/mem).

LLVM provides atomic operations, including unordered operations intended to
support safe languages, but their ordering, widths and target support matter.
Unordered atomicity alone does not publish an initialized object or protect its
lifetime. The safe implementation must use the required synchronization, locks or
snapshots and preserve it through lowering; ordinary unsynchronized access and
optimistic alias promises are not substitutes. Unsupported operations need a
defined fallback or a diagnostic, including on Wasm and GPU targets.
[LLVM atomics](https://llvm.org/docs/Atomics.html#unordered).

The memory/consistency profile belongs in compilation and cache identity. Strict
compile-time execution still needs identical results for identical explicit inputs.
Runtime scheduling nondeterminism cannot silently become a compile-time input:
reject it in strict evaluation or provide a deterministic execution policy and
explicit tracked inputs. Known-value evaluation continues to invoke ordinary
Tower code with the same contracts, not an independent folding pass.

What today's work contributes and what remains:

Compiler worlds, shared entity identity, private worker scratch, component access
claims, pinned views, staged publication, dependency continuations and drain-before-
release rules are relevant implementation groundwork. They make the required
ownership boundaries visible. They currently rely on manually correct Tower code
and include raw pointers. A pinned view is not a payload lock. Completing the ECS
conversion would not itself produce a safe user language, an enforced borrow/effect
system, safe collections, or a specified optional concurrency model.

A reasonable future sequence is: specify the safety/profile and trusted boundary;
build scoped safe world/handle APIs and initialized owned containers in Tower;
enforce non-escape, alias/access and transitive effect rules on shared nodes;
connect those checked capabilities to the scheduler; then add narrowly specified
concurrent operations where useful. Explicit initialization, typed absence/results,
aggregate ownership/returns and access effects are useful language prerequisites.
Compile-time generation can derive wrappers and access plans, but generated code
must pass the same checks. No privileged syntax-only shortcut.

Future focused tests should try stale/cross-world handles, generation exhaustion,
remove/re-add, archetype movement during access, duplicate mutable access,
partially initialized containers, escaping callbacks, concurrent removal,
cancellation and generated/imported unsafe access. Compare interpreter and native
behavior under the same profile and benchmark realistic traversal/update loads.
These are proposed acceptance criteria, not tests run for this documentation turn.

Conclusion of this assessment: a convenient memory-safe ECS-oriented language
above Tower is credible and aligns with the earlier notes. The strongest fit is
typed access plus scoped runtime protection, allowing static proofs to eliminate
cost where possible. Optional logical races are feasible under explicit safe
operations. Stronghold remains future work; current ECS/threading and ordinary
interpreter compile-time execution remain the implementation priority.

### 2026-11-21 — Stronghold revision: static guarantees and cheap scoped access

The user clarifies the priority behind the earlier safe-handle explorations:
memory safety with very little overhead, enforced at compile time wherever
possible, using ECS-aware language features to avoid pervasive lifetime/type
ceremony. Entity handles should become direct pointers while safely borrowed;
safe memory chunks outside ECS should remain possible. This refines the preceding
Stronghold proposal. It does not request implementation yet or relax memory/type
safety. Compiler ECS/threading and interpreter-based compile-time work remain the
implementation priority; all future project-owned implementation remains Tower.

Change in emphasis:

Make static ownership, access and non-escape rules the primary mechanism. Runtime
checks, locks, reference counting and reclamation schemes from the earlier entry
are tools for explicitly dynamic cases, not the default cost of every reference.
The desired common case is a bounded access scope whose correctness is checked
once by the compiler, with any necessary runtime admission at its boundary and
ordinary pointer loads/stores inside. Do not build an always-checked reference
system and hope LLVM removes all its overhead. Define eligible cases and their
lowering costs explicitly, then verify the generated code.

Keep four concepts separate: a persistent entity handle denotes identity; a
temporary typed borrow grants access; a scope keeps the underlying storage alive
and stable; and an access capability controls conflicting reads/writes. A handle
need not own or pin an entity. A borrow may lower to one target pointer once its
scope and permissions are established. Bounds metadata for a slice is still real
runtime data when its length is dynamic; erasing ownership metadata does not mean
all useful types become one machine word.

Proposed default ECS contract:

1. Enter a system/query with statically checked read/write requirements and an
   owner/world context. Infer requirements through ordinary calls, including
   callbacks and generated functions. Public or separately compiled boundaries
   expose checked summaries so callers do not need to inspect every body.
2. Partition compatible work into disjoint entity/table ranges. Give each job
   scoped access to its ranges. Multiple readers are compatible; mutable access
   must be exclusive for the actual overlapping storage. A read/write component
   set is the initial conservative model, with proven filters/ranges recovering
   concurrency. Readiness dependencies and access conflicts both constrain jobs.
3. Hold structural changes that could invalidate those ranges until their users
   finish. Updating fields is distinct from moving entities, changing membership,
   resizing borrowed storage or freeing owners. Structural access is an effect
   that ordinary row code does not possess. Queue commands explicitly or leave
   the access scope before acquiring structural authority.
4. Traverse existing matched rows directly. The iterator already proves entity
   existence and component presence for that protected traversal, so it need not
   look up a generational handle for every row or field. Disjoint chunk iterators
   can establish independent mutable borrows by construction. Scoped borrowed
   references cannot be stored beyond their scope or retained by an escaping
   callback. Borrow shortening should follow last use where provable, not always
   the end of a function.
5. Join the relevant jobs, end their borrows, then publish changes in the specified
   order. This is a deliberate execution contract. Do not silently postpone a
   synchronous mutation whose immediate visibility the program depends on. A
   command's visibility and same-batch lookup semantics must be documented.

This can amortize lifetime/structural protection across thousands of accesses.
When exclusive ownership and structured job lifetime already prove the scope,
the access token can be a compiler-only fact: no per-object pin counter, heap
guard allocation or reference-count traffic is inherently required. A dynamic
shared-world scheduler may still need admission bookkeeping and synchronization
per job or batch. Those costs do not disappear because the compiler verified
correct use of its protocol. Starting with world-wide structural phases is simple;
later narrow them to affected stores/tables/allocations where measured benefits
justify the additional ownership rules. Adding a component may move several
columns, so merely locking that component's type is not sufficient.

Pinning also needs a precise meaning here. Freezing a component's location does
not freeze a vector allocation reached through one of its fields, nor grant
permission to race on its contents. Track ownership and invalidating effects for
reachable storage: buffer growth, nested container replacement and callbacks can
invalidate borrows independently of archetype movement. Shared references inside
different components can alias the same resource. Access summaries must include
that resource/region or conservatively reject conflicting use. Component names
alone cannot prove arbitrary pointer graphs disjoint.

Static proof versus runtime facts:

| Operation | Proposed proof/admission | Intended repeated-access cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Visit matched query rows | Checked query capabilities, stable membership, disjoint ranges | Direct column/payload access; no handle validation per field |
| Resolve an arbitrary saved handle | Check world/incarnation/presence within a protected scope unless already proven | Lookup once per acquired borrow, then direct access |
| Visit an owned buffer | Owner stays live; iterator constrains initialized range | Ordinary traversal, with bounds checks absent when proven redundant |
| Split a buffer for parallel jobs | Validate a dynamic split boundary once, construct disjoint views | Direct access in each view under its range contract |
| Mutate two arbitrary entity IDs | Prove IDs/ranges distinct or check aliasing when acquiring access | Direct access after successful admission |
| Publish a genuinely shared mutable value | Explicit atomic/lock/snapshot contract | Its documented synchronization cost remains |

The compiler can prove that every use follows a safe protocol without knowing
which entities a runtime file or network packet will identify. It cannot generally
prove that an arbitrary saved handle is still alive, that two runtime IDs differ,
or that a runtime index is in bounds. A successful check can establish a fact for
the remainder of a protected scope; checking again on every field is unnecessary.
Removing all such checks requires restricting the operation or changing ownership
so the fact follows by construction. A static-only subset can reject operations
without those proofs; useful dynamic APIs can retain an explicit checked boundary.
Never convert proof failure into unchecked access in optimized builds.

Ergonomics to target:

Ordinary system authors should write typed component inputs, a familiar loop and
ordinary helper calls. Infer scoped lifetimes, read/write effects and temporary
borrows; generate query/partition plans. Persistent graph edges use copyable
handles, so users do not encode an entire evolving entity graph into nested
reference lifetimes. Returning an owned value, keeping a handle, splitting a
region or moving structural changes to a command phase should be straightforward
fixes with concrete diagnostics. Advanced library authors may need explicit
ownership/effect contracts; do not pretend every relationship can be inferred.

We still need restrictions on aliasing, escape, destruction and mutation. ECS
offers useful structural constraints that can make them easier to express; it
does not make unrestricted shared mutation statically safe. Avoid compensating
for a rejected proof with hidden copies, reference counting, global locks or an
unexplained loss of parallelism. Expose consequential costs at API boundaries.
Measure both programmer friction and runtime performance rather than declaring
the result universally easier or faster than Rust before implementing it.

Compile-time facilities that help:

Use ordinary Tower type values and functions to describe component schemas,
query shapes, ownership and access requirements. Known schemas can generate
specialized traversal, layout access and job descriptors at compile time. Erase
proof-only region/permission information when valid, while keeping runtime world
checks where the instance identity is dynamic. Compile-time knowledge of a type
does not establish the identity or liveness of every runtime object of that type.

Ownership, definite initialization, non-escape and effect checking operate on
the shared entities. Their reusable summaries should be dependency queries with
explicit invalidation, independent work scheduled in parallel and deterministic
diagnostics. Recursive calls require convergent effect-summary analysis where
supported, not declaring every call-graph cycle illegal. Keep the proof system
small and predictable initially: owned regions, scoped borrows, access sets and
disjoint iterator/split operations, rather than an arbitrary theorem prover.

These are static safety analyses, not a separate constant-propagation evaluator.
When an expression's actual known value is needed, use ordinary interpreter
evaluation under Tower's existing deterministic contract. LLVM can optimize the
resulting ordinary operations. Generated code must satisfy the same safety rules;
user code cannot fabricate a proof or capability by returning a convenient flag.
Foundation remains the compilable semantic representation, and safe module/trust
contracts must survive or be rechecked at separate compilation and import.

Safe allocations outside ECS are part of the design:

- An owned allocation or buffer has one destruction authority. Move the owner
  when transferring it; create temporary read-only or exclusive writable views
  for access. Release occurs at the defined ownership boundary. This can compile
  to an allocation, pointer/length storage and a matching free, without a mandatory
  refcount or ECS entity per allocation. Aggregate move/destruction semantics
  must be defined first; current Tower vector_move is a raw caller contract.
- An arena/region owns a group of stable allocations and releases them together
  after all external borrows/jobs end. Internal graphs can contain cycles without
  per-edge reference counts. Initial restrictions can forbid individual frees
  and moving live allocations; adding those operations later requires stronger
  identities or proofs. Transfer an isolated region between jobs only when no
  incompatible references remain. Ownership metadata concerns the region, not
  every object in it.
- Safe slices retain length and a lifetime tied to their owner. Splitting creates
  disjoint child permissions. Resizing or disposing the owner is unavailable while
  conflicting views are live. A user can hold a stable owner for a long computation
  without manufacturing ECS entities for temporary numerical buffers or parser
  scratch. Shared non-ECS resources can use the same scheduler access model.
- Initialization means no read of an uninitialized/invalid value, not compulsory
  zero-fill followed by overwriting every element. Permit an inaccessible builder
  to allocate raw backing storage and construct each element once; expose only
  the initialized range, and publish the completed typed buffer after its contract
  is satisfied. Track partial cleanup correctly on failure. Prefer append/exact-
  length construction protocols over an initialization bitmap for every object.
  Arbitrary partially initialized typed reads remain unavailable to safe code.

Safe byte buffers do not authorize reinterpreting arbitrary bytes as references
or invariant-bearing structs. Typed decoding/construction, alignment and checked
layout arithmetic still matter. Address-stable allocations do not alone prevent
use-after-free or writable aliases. Optional shared ownership/concurrent buffers
remain available with visible costs rather than becoming the ordinary model.

Optional logical races remain a separate future feature. The default query/owned-
region path should prevent conflicting ordinary accesses. Relaxing consistency
must not force every hot-path load to become atomic, or silently change strict
compile-time execution into a nondeterministic computation. The earlier examples
of absent lookup results and protected snapshots remain valid for opted-in APIs.

Evidence and current implementation limits:

Reviewed scaffolding/library/entities.tower: today's Entity is a raw pointer to
an object containing store/id/reference metadata. EntityView is heap allocated,
increments the store's view count, and delays reclamation; its own comment says
payload access still needs permissions. Dense table columns point to stable
component payloads rather than guaranteeing packed contiguous payload arrays.
scaffolding/library/vector.tower and docs/borrowed-iteration.md explicitly leave
growth/borrow safety to the caller. Thus the proposed generational safe handles,
erased scoped capabilities, contiguous-query cost targets and safe owned buffers
must not be described as implemented properties of those current APIs. Existing
coordinator-owned view/stage machinery is a starting point, not a requirement
to preserve its allocation/bookkeeping cost in Stronghold.

Primary references reviewed for specific mechanisms, not performance promises:
Bevy's [DeferredWorld](https://docs.rs/bevy_ecs/latest/bevy_ecs/world/struct.DeferredWorld.html)
separates component access from structural mutation, and its
[SystemParam contract](https://docs.rs/bevy_ecs/latest/bevy_ecs/system/trait.SystemParam.html#safety)
requires complete access registration and conflict prevention. Its
[get_entity_mut](https://docs.rs/bevy_ecs/latest/bevy_ecs/world/struct.World.html#method.get_entity_mut)
also reports duplicate mutable entity requests, illustrating why dynamic aliasing
needs an acquisition rule. Rust's
[split_at_mut](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.slice.html#method.split_at_mut)
constructs nonoverlapping mutable slices after a boundary check. Pony's
[reference capabilities](https://tutorial.ponylang.io/reference-capabilities/reference-capabilities.html)
show compiler-enforced isolation/immutable sharing, including isolated groups
with internal references. We are borrowing these principles, not adopting their
full languages, runtime memory management or syntax.

Revised future implementation order and acceptance criteria:

1. Specify scoped access, structural effects, owned buffers and moves, including
   initialized construction and cleanup. Define a small trusted implementation
   boundary and the common ergonomic query/region APIs together.
2. Enforce those rules on the shared graph; infer summaries and connect proven
   access to dependency/job scheduling. Add dynamic handle acquisition only where
   necessary. Support non-ECS owned storage from the start.
3. Implement a representative component update and parallel buffer operation in
   Tower. Compare to equivalent raw Tower code with identical layout, arithmetic,
   synchronization and optimized backend settings. Inspect optimized loops for
   per-element checks, allocations, refcount updates and synchronization; measure
   whole-job throughput and compiler cost too. No benchmark has been run here.
4. Reject escaping borrows, conflicting dynamic aliases, structural mutation and
   nested-buffer growth during access, early arena release and uninitialized

final `..default`. Every field is required unless that explicit zero baseline is
present. Fields bind existing declarations on the shared entities; duplicate,
unknown and missing fields and exact type mismatches have source diagnostics.
Declarations and aggregate reset destinations lower to existing Foundation stores
and optional fill, with one destination evaluation and source-order field

needs call/alias/escape summaries, provenance for generated temporaries, and policy
identity in cache contracts. That strict validator is not implemented here. A
plain declaration still leaves storage uninitialized. Checking completeness is
separate from storage lowering, so stricter validation need not alter Foundation.

### 2026-11-21 - Next language slice after named-field initialization

Pulled main with `git pull --rebase`; e8661dd was already current. Reviewed the
language plan, simplification audit, named-initialization contract and current
compiler/library sources in response to the user's next-feature question. This
is a recommendation, not an implementation or a new measured migration count.

Recommend struct return values first, with construction into caller-provided
destination storage. Named-field initialization can populate that destination,
but semantic_statements.tower still explicitly rejects struct parameters and
returns, while semantic_values.tower rejects aggregate value copies. The gap is
visible in regex_lowering.tower's RegexFragment output parameters and in the
work graph's WorkTicket output APIs. vector_pop, stack_pop and queue_pop also
use bool plus an output pointer; their empty/failure cases need an absence/result
contract rather than an unconditional struct return. Output-named parameters in
formatters and semantic workers also include append buffers and persistent job
state, so they are not automatically return-value migration candidates.

The first bounded implementation should permit fully initialized plain records
returned directly into a declaration or another return destination, without
requiring arbitrary aggregate copying. Specify destination aliasing, evaluation
and cleanup order, recursive calls and target layout. Preserve owned-resource
constructors and explicit transfers; pointer fields alone do not prove that a
record is non-owning. Returning an existing owner, replacement and aggregate
arguments need explicit move/borrow/drop contracts before broad adoption.

Lower internal return destinations to existing typed pointer parameters, stores,
calls and void returns on the shared Foundation entities. This is a proposed
Tower calling convention, not a claim of native external aggregate ABI support.
Keep source signature/provenance metadata on the same ECS nodes, discover the
signature/layout dependencies through the existing work graph, and use existing
worker stages with deterministic publication. Implement and test in Tower only;
validate recursive/forward calls, lifetime/alias cases, Foundation round trips,
both interpreters, LLVM and worker-count output/diagnostic equivalence. Publish
the compatible bootstrap before migrating compiler callers.

Then add ordinary tagged result(T, E)/option(T), exhaustive payload matching and
finally explicit try propagation once active-payload ownership and early-return
cleanup are defined. This follows the existing errors-as-values plan and targets
repeated status/output/error plumbing. Exact overloads and receiver-call sugar
remain useful, but struct returns unlock these larger API improvements. Actual
line reductions require a subsequent reviewed migration; no savings or speedup
are claimed from this source inspection.

Validation for this recommendation is source/document review and `git diff
--check`. No compiler inputs changed. Documentation publication reuses the
verified runtime assets and retains their build-source identity.

### 2026-11-21 — Struct values and ordinary named binding inference

The user requested C-style struct values, then rejected the existing `const`
shorthand after discovering that it generated zero-argument functions. The final
direction is ordinary `var` bindings, separate immutability and staging proofs,
and named values/enums instead of magic numbers. Foundation's existing declaration
rule is reused. An initial Tower declaration override merely marked candidates;
it was removed after review because the initializer already carries Tower surface
metadata. No Foundation/Bedrock grammar extension is required. All implementation,
fixtures and the migration tool are Tower; existing browser test transport only
loads the added Tower fixtures. No new C++/Python implementation was introduced.

Struct checking now admits same-nominal-type initialization, assignment, arguments
and returns, including inferred locals, generic calls, nested arrays, empty structs
and named/default construction in value contexts. Signature metadata stays on the
function entity. Coordinator publication rewrites internal executable signatures
to existing Foundation pointer arguments/result parameters before independent
lowering workers run. Fieldwise snapshots preserve left-to-right argument order,
single destination evaluation, aliases/self-assignment and return-before-defer.
Copies preserve pointer addresses, not pointed-to ownership or padding bytes.
Extern/export aggregate signatures require an explicit pointer ABI; standalone
array values remain unsupported. No platform struct ABI or copy-elision promise.

The first aggregate trial aborted when a body worker discovered an unprepared
by-value layout under a pinned view. Declaration/header dependencies now prepare
those layouts before admission. A legacy print-struct negative fixture also
exposed a diagnostic-offset regression; restored the operand source span while
updating its message. Aggregate return-flow validation retains the source result
type after executable signatures become void. Temporary fields are readable but
cannot be assigned/addressed as durable source locations. New test failures use
descriptive messages rather than unexplained numeric IDs; the touched semantic
oracle case uses a named enum member and the parameter limit is named.

`SemanticKnownBinding` records owner, source ordinal, immutability and observation
ordering on the declaration entity. Writes, modifications and address exposure
invalidate fixed-binding eligibility. A conservative source-order walk includes
callees and prevents substitution across earlier global observations. Eligible
integer/bool candidates create ordinary evaluation jobs, with cloned initializer
entities owning their lowering output. Interpreter inputs reference those jobs;
reads suspend on dependencies, while a called function's own locals retain their
actual frame storage. Optional failure leaves runtime code intact; explicit
`comptime` still diagnoses unsupported captures/effects. Publication follows joins
and writes typed literals into canonical Foundation. There is no alternate math
evaluator. Mutable locals inside staged calls work normally. Pointer/aggregate
constant materialization and general tracked effects are still future work.

An initial implementation allocated metadata kinds even for Foundation-only
programs, changing recorded entity graph fingerprints despite no candidate values.
Creating kinds lazily on the first Tower candidate restored the oracle. Temporary
hash-debug output then exposed that the native execution test transport does not
link Tower's guest print adapter; removed that temporary instrumentation. Rebased
onto 459b199, preserving the baseline native retirement and resumable control-body
work; resolved the browser fixture-list conflict by retaining both sides.

Native development environment: Docker `tower-c-validation`, `/work` checkout,
LLVM/Clang 19, build `/cache/struct-values`, documented pinned predecessor
961952b73e4e9e1d9d08556c3a7f651ae8457c76cbc4c70d7f72d80f5c857742.

followed by `tower-execution-tests /work/scaffolding` passed the new suites, both

and all recorded semantic oracle fixtures (`build/known-values-integrated.log`).
Earlier struct native graph/fast/LLVM execution also printed 0. A final affected
run includes the temporary-location rejection and descriptive fixture messages;
its receipt and release validation follow below.

#### Library initialization integration

The first published pin accepts and folds ordinary named bindings, but the actual
migration's fresh library build exposed a missing cleanup step: folded declarations
and generated initializer temporaries still appeared as top-level executable
statements, rejected by `backend_lower` in library mode. The migration was kept
local/stashed; published sources still use the supported earlier spelling.

Each binding's existing lowering worker now records its emitted initializer range
on the declaration component. After successful strict evaluation and substitution
of all reads, coordinator publication removes that complete range and dead local
index entries. Failed/mutable/effectful candidates are untouched. This avoids a
special library evaluator, hidden initializer or backend-only semantics. The first
cleanup trial preserved byte offsets but forgot to renumber surviving local slot
indices, producing LLVM references into another function's local table (and a
native fault). Renumbering the derived per-function slot indexes fixes that issue;
published byte offsets remain stable for surviving storage. A dedicated
`known_binding_library.tower` fixture covers literal, computed, conditional and
local named values through an exported entry point, plus graph/round-trip checks
that no runtime module initialization remains. This fix requires another pinned
bootstrap before the stashed compiler migration can be published.

The library object now links with Clang 19 and its exported main exits 0 without
any initializer wrapper. The complete native execution suite passes after slot
renumbering (`binding-library-index-tests.log`), including both feature suites,
both target widths and prior semantic oracles. LLVM execution of the named-binding
fixture also prints 0 after initializer removal.

from implementation 2b65c3e. Its documented default bootstrap path builds a fresh

library fixture links/runs without initialization and both value fixtures pass.

Retired const syntax is not promoted. New test cases are Tower text plus scope
assertions in comments, run by the existing vscode-tmgrammar-test 0.1.3 engine.
There is no new JavaScript/Python/native validation implementation. A path-filtered
GitHub Actions workflow runs npm ci and the same tests on main and pull requests.

#### Import-cycle integration

The next migration build passed runtime-library production, then reached an older
frontend restriction: cyclic compiler modules allowed function/type declarations
but rejected every `CoreDeclare` before its value could be checked. The error
originated in `syntax_emission_types` / `format_syntax_preview`. Kept migration
local again and extended the existing module ownership metadata with cycle status.
Frontend cycle validation now defers ordinary variable declarations, while still
rejecting grammar updates and executable statements. After normal inference and
initializer removal, semantic validation rejects any surviving global declaration
owned by a cyclic module. No literal-only parser evaluator or special constant
declaration syntax was added. Positive cyclic modules share fixed scalar bindings;
negative fixtures retain an effectful initializer and must diagnose the absent
dependency-first initialization order. The same tests include Foundation round
trips. Publish this compatible reader before adopting the migration.

#### First required-tool port: LLD compatibility

`scaffolding/tools/lld_compat.tower` owns the exact-match patch decision and host
file operation; `prepare_lld_compat.tower` supplies the Linux/POSIX CLI. It reuses
`ByteBuffer`, `bytes_*`, the existing `driver_read_file`/`driver_write_file` and
Tower UTF-8 validator. No ECS entities are needed for a byte-string operation.
File effects happen only when the tool runs. Paths are arguments, never shell
commands. The fixed upstream patch still uses `WasmPageSize` and excludes PIC;
this is third-party compatibility, not new native Tower implementation.

The port matches the predecessor's universal-newline read, marker/anchor guards,
idempotence and failure status. Missing/duplicate anchors, an existing upstream
symbol and an altered patch reject without opening the file for writing. A
no-op preserves the original bytes, including CRLF. Buffer publication happens
after successful allocation, supports an aliased input/output, and explicitly
transfers ownership. A physical write/close failure reports failure and may
leave partial bytes, like the existing driver helper; atomic filesystem replace
and concurrent mutation protection are not claimed. Invalid UTF-8 is rejected.
Usage now produces a concise message and exit 2; operational errors use exit 1.

Validation environment: Windows PowerShell invoking Ubuntu WSL as `trevo`,
Clang/LLVM 19, own caches `/home/trevo/.cache/tower/agent1-tooling-*`. Installed
the checked-in pin with `python3 bootstrap/install.py --cache
/home/trevo/.cache/tower/agent1-tooling-bootstrap`; archive SHA-256 is
`083b7da564f33389f4ca512829e0d50a3982e76632a65d5bbe8dbb683c2f3f35`.
No private `TOWER_BOOTSTRAP_COMPILER` environment override was used. The CMake
argument below names that verified installation explicitly for the isolated
runtime-library target, not an unpublished compiler.

Reproduction (Linux shell, repository root; `pin` abbreviates the installation
path above and `out` the isolated `agent1-tooling-native` cache):

```sh
cmake -S . -B "$out" -G Ninja -DTOWER_NATIVE=ON \
  -DTOWER_BOOTSTRAP_COMPILER="$pin/towerc" \
  -DCMAKE_PROJECT_scaffolding_INCLUDE="$PWD/cmake/TowerBackend.cmake" \
  -DLLVM_DIR=/usr/lib/llvm-19/lib/cmake/llvm -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=/usr/bin/clang-19 -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=/usr/bin/clang++-19
cmake --build "$out" --target tower-guest-host-library --parallel 2
"$pin/towerc" scaffolding/tools/prepare_lld_compat.tower --library \
  --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu --bedrock scaffolding/bedrock.tower \
  --foundation scaffolding/foundation.tower -o "$out/prepare_lld_compat.o"
clang-19 "$out/prepare_lld_compat.o" "$out/guest-host-library.o" -o "$out/prepare_lld_compat"
"$pin/towerc" scaffolding/tests/lld_compat_checks.tower --library \
  --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu --bedrock scaffolding/bedrock.tower \
  --foundation scaffolding/foundation.tower -o "$out/lld_compat_checks.o"
clang-19 "$out/lld_compat_checks.o" "$out/guest-host-library.o" -o "$out/lld_compat_checks"
"$out/lld_compat_checks" "$out/fixture.cpp"
```

#### Bounded inferred evaluation before final migration

With the cycle-aware pin, the actual compiler migration builds natively through
the default bootstrap (`value-bindings-migrated.log`). Updated 263 declarations
and callers across 177 Tower files, removed the two constant grammar rules,
updated embedded module examples, and began replacing complete typed worker/type
copies with ordinary struct assignments. These changes remain local until the
release checks pass. The native suite's retired-syntax test assumed an
"Unexpected" parser diagnostic; the actual useful message is "Missing '?' before
'old'" after `const` becomes an ordinary identifier. Corrected that assertion.

The single-thread browser build succeeded, but the larger threaded parser compiler
exceeded the existing Foundation component budget while instantiating
`vector_reserve` from `lr_append`. Automatic inference was cloning initializers and
allocating evaluation work even when their inputs were known runtime parameters
or mutable/address-exposed bindings. Added a read-only eligibility scan before
those allocations. It uses the existing immutability/order facts and does no
arithmetic, call execution or folding. Eligible unresolved inputs still go through
the ordinary interpreter/dependency graph. The resource limit is unchanged.
Stashed the complete migration while rebuilding/publishing this reader improvement;
the published old-spelling compiler remains buildable throughout.

The native execution suite passes with eligibility filtering, including explicit
capture/effect failures, dependency cycles, both target widths, worker determinism
and prior semantic oracles (`binding-budget-tests.log`).

Before final publication, review found that effect freedom alone is insufficient
for automatic substitution: an otherwise pure helper can convert its local
address to an integer or compare addresses, observing interpreter placement instead
of runtime placement. Inferred invocations now request relocation-independent
results. The same strict interpreter refuses pointer/integer conversions and
pointer comparisons for that optional evaluation; the runtime calculation remains.
Explicit `comptime` invocations retain their existing target-address policy, so an
explicitly staged scalar initializer is still a valid known input. Added rejection
tests for implicitly inferred address integers and address comparison. Arithmetic,
loads/stores and call execution still use the ordinary handlers; there is no
separate evaluator or host-address serialization.

The first address-comparison test used `<`, which the current pointer type checker
already rejects as requiring integer operands. Changed the eligibility regression
to supported pointer equality; pointer ordering/difference belongs in the C-level
completeness audit rather than being silently claimed as implemented here.

The final relocation-eligibility suite passes all native execution, Foundation
round-trip, worker-count and semantic oracle checks
(`binding-relocatable-final-tests.log`).

### 2026-11-21: in-house archive tooling and the non-Tower dependency policy

Continued agent 1's tooling assignment after the first pushed milestone
`f0cac4f`. The interrupted preparation turn made no file changes; the resumed
work rechecked the clean checkout, pulled, and read the coordinator's current
ownership notice. The user clarified that "third party language" meant
project-owned code in languages other than Tower, not upstream libraries.
Later the user specifically rejected a new zlib link for this tool and requested
a concise general preference in `AGENTS.md`: implement new libraries in Tower
where practical, starting with a correct minimal subset that can grow; necessary
OS/platform calls remain external. Added that instruction under implementation
language. It does not claim existing upstream dependencies have been replaced.

The coordinator's `92da0a8` source milestone was pulled during implementation.
`git ls-files '*.cpp' '*.c' '*.h' '*.hpp'` is empty, `host/legacy.tower` exists,
and the default pin is now Tower-built Linux x64, archive SHA-256
`fd536ba1ae5cefe891e78690e23c06ef7fcd5d729c0e3395824d8977abf9a9b4`.
Read the changed AGENTS/bootstrap contracts. This is the canonical Linux/Docker
route, not proof of native Windows/macOS release execution. The coordinator
still owns the active release scripts, bootstrap and publication lock until its
hosted validation completes; this milestone adds independent tools/libraries
without swapping those paths or modifying its pin.

#### Implemented components and boundaries

* `library/crc32.tower`: incremental IEEE CRC-32 over explicit bytes, with fixed
  width arithmetic and no host service.
* `library/zip_archive.tower`: deterministic single-disk ZIP32 writer for stored
  and raw-DEFLATE payloads. Callers explicitly supply order, timestamps, flags,
  attributes and compression. It checks complete archive limits before payload
  access, rejects duplicate/unsafe relative member paths and unsupported flags,
  and publishes output ownership only on success. Inputs may borrow the previous
  destination. ZIP64, encryption, archive reading and filename transcoding are
  outside this first writer; callers supply the name bytes in their stated encoding.
* `library/deflate.tower`: pure Tower raw RFC 1951 encoder, using fixed Huffman
  codes, a 32 KiB LZ77 window, 4,096 hash buckets and a 64-candidate search budget.
  Each match is at most 258 bytes; nearest equal-length matches win. Absolute
  offsets and decreasing chain checks bound traversal after the ring wraps.
  Stored blocks win when fixed coding would be larger, limiting expansion to
  five bytes per 65,535-byte block (one block for an empty input). Scratch is
  private to each call; allocation/rejection leaves the destination intact.
  No dynamic-Huffman optimizer, streaming API, dictionaries, inflater or zlib/gzip
  wrapper is claimed. This is a reusable initial compression subset, not all of zlib.
* `tools/roku_package.tower` and `package_roku.tower`: preserve the three-file
  package recipe, source marker/UTF-8 checks, universal-newline normalization,
  entry order, 2020-01-01 timestamp and Unix 0644 attributes. Compression now uses
  the Tower codec. `tool_files_posix.tower` provides explicit runtime parent
  creation and `realpath`-based source/output protection, including symlinks.
  There is no command-shell interpolation. The CLI uses Linux/POSIX filesystem
  APIs; the byte/CRC/compression/archive libraries have no platform ABI.

Source/output protection follows the predecessor's resolved-path rule; hard-link
identity and concurrent path mutation are not claimed. A failed physical write
can leave partial output, as in the existing driver helper. A failed compression
allocation preserves the caller's output but deterministic allocation-failure
injection was not added to this standalone suite. Names and files are ordinary
tool data, so no second semantic graph or unnecessary ECS entities were introduced.

Primary format references used for implementation:
[PKWARE APPNOTE 6.3.10](https://pkware.cachefly.net/webdocs/casestudies/APPNOTE.TXT)
and [RFC 1951](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1951.html).
The writer follows the local/central/end record layout; the codec separates
Huffman bit order from ordinary numeric fields and handles overlapping copies.

#### Trials, rejected approach and verification

The first unpublished draft used the existing system zlib runtime through
`compress2` and removed the RFC 1950 wrapper. It produced an archive identical
to the Python predecessor (SHA-256 `006c0d8688ae8c85546c6759f787de3cc62f162071e8241b9c9f82775ea8d748`).
That was useful compatibility evidence, but the user preferred an in-house
implementation. Deleted the draft host adapter before commit and removed both
production and test zlib links. **The earlier byte-identical compressed-output
result applies only to that discarded draft.** The final Tower codec deliberately
uses a different compression strategy; exact decompressed content and metadata
are the compatibility contract. `readelf -d package_roku` now lists only
`libc.so.6` as NEEDED, with no zlib or LLVM dependency in the tool executable.

Other failed trials: the published language currently has no hexadecimal literal
syntax or `u16`, so protocol values use named decimal `u32` bindings and checked
16-bit field limits. Fixed-array bounds do not accept ordinary known bindings at
this stage; the fixed-size recipe uses explicitly owned allocations instead.
Numeric `convert` checks range, so emitting low bytes must mask before conversion;
the initial unmasked writer trapped and was corrected before any successful ZIP
claim. `else if` requires a nested block under the current grammar. The Docker
configure invocation initially split an unquoted PowerShell CMake argument at
`.cmake`; quoting the whole `-D` argument fixed it. No compiler semantics were
changed for these tooling issues.

`tool_archive_checks.tower` passes exact CRC check-vector/chunking checks; ZIP
repeatability, complete-size limits, empty archive, invalid and duplicate paths,
unsupported encryption, metadata overflow, ZIP64 rejection before reading data,
and input/output aliasing. Roku checks cover UTF-8/marker failures, unchanged
failure destinations, LF/CRLF/lone-CR normalization, actual file writes,
same-path and symlink output rejection, and a file used as a parent directory.
CLI usage returns 2; missing source and source/output equality return 1.
Paths containing spaces and literal `;$(no_command)` were passed without a shell
and written as literal filesystem names.

`deflate_checks.tower` generates **161 members** and their independent original
files. Cases include empty and short input, seeded binary noise, runs, all byte
values, a repeated 32 KiB window, 257/258/259 lengths, both sides of 32 KiB and
65,535-byte boundaries, and inputs spanning multiple stored blocks. It also
constructs both endpoints of every RFC length/distance range to exercise coding
independently of match search. The encoder checks repeatability, aliased output,
and the stored expansion bound; the standard Python ZIP reader independently
validates CRC/decompression, then `diff -r expected actual` compares every byte.
Both WSL and the canonical Docker image pass these checks. Corpus SHA-256:
`e69c5e83922aacdf254b29da9980597a96938625cb9787203e452c9f37c0577d`.
No Python implementation/test helper was added: only the existing Python package
command and standard `python3 -m zipfile` reader were used as external references.

Started the next floating-point audit, recorded in the language roadmap. Existing
foreign-name mangling recognizes float/double, but no floating scalar kind or
executable value operations exist. Proposed a Tower-owned deterministic binary
kernel before integrating shared scalar components, staging and backend emission.
The proposed strict policy distinguishes bit-preserving copies/sign changes from
canonicalized binary arithmetic NaNs. Primary research:
[WebAssembly numeric semantics](https://webassembly.github.io/spec/core/exec/numerics.html)
and [SoftFloat's documented interface](https://www.jhauser.us/arithmetic/SoftFloat-3/doc/SoftFloat.html).

of Tower's required deterministic bits. No floating language feature or C parity
is claimed by this research checkpoint. No new C++, Python or JavaScript logic
was introduced; the only additional JS transport edit removed a stale call.

Coordinator completion at `669a6ad` released the active build/package paths.

`build-llvm.sh` invokes Tower `prepare_lld_compat`; the Roku guide invokes
